title: Vibration: how strings, skins and air columns make sound

summary.text: Draw a card slowly along a comb and you hear separate ticks, but draw it fast and the ticks join into one steady note. Why? In this unit you will count the pushes in each second with a comb, watch a slow string vibrate, and hear a spoon ring through a string.
summary.art: A child drawing a card along the teeth of a comb, with a row of separate dots on the left that crowd together into one smooth line on the right.

intro.hook: Pluck a rubber band stretched over a steel tumbler. It hums, and it looks like a blur. Touch it with one finger, and the hum stops at once. What was the band doing while it hummed? And why did it keep doing it after your finger let go?
intro.text: The band was vibrating. It was moving back and forth far too quickly for your eyes to follow. In this unit you slow that movement down until you can watch it. You turn separate ticks into a note with a comb. You work out how many pushes reach your ear each second. You make grains jump on a skin that nothing touches. You hear a spoon ring like a temple bell through a piece of string. By the end you can say what vibrates in a veena, a mridangam, a bansuri and your own throat.
intro.art: A rubber band stretched over the open mouth of a steel tumbler, drawn as a blur that is widest in the middle, with a child's finger about to touch it.

outcomes: I can say what a vibration is, using the words rest position, amplitude and frequency.
I can explain why a plucked string keeps moving back and forth, and what makes a vibration faster or slower.
I can explain how separate pushes become a steady note, and work out the pushes in each second, in hertz.
I can say what vibrates in a string instrument, a drum, a wind instrument and a voice.
I can describe how a vibration travels through a solid, a liquid or a gas to the eardrum.
I can plan a fair test, and name what I change, what I measure and what I keep the same.
I can explain where a vibration goes when a sound dies away, and why a soundboard makes a sound louder.

terms.meaning: A movement back and forth, repeated again and again. One vibration is one full trip: away, back through the middle, to the other side and back again.
terms.example: A plucked veena string vibrates. So does a drum skin after it is struck.
terms.art: A string fixed at both ends, drawn in three positions: curved up, straight, and curved down, with arrows between them.

terms.meaning: The place where a thing stays when nothing is moving it. A vibrating thing moves to each side of its rest position.
terms.example: A rubber band's rest position is the straight line it makes before you pluck it.
terms.art: A straight rubber band between two fingers with a dotted line along it labelled 'rest position'.

terms.meaning: The size of a vibration: how far the thing moves from its rest position. A bigger amplitude gives a louder sound.
terms.example: Pluck a string gently and the blur is thin. Pluck it harder and the blur is wide, and the sound is louder.
terms.art: Two blurred strings side by side, one thin and one wide, each with a small arrow from the middle line to the edge of the blur.

terms.meaning: The number of vibrations in one second. A higher frequency gives a higher note.
terms.example: A honeybee's wings beat about 230 times a second. That frequency is the hum you hear.
terms.art: A stopwatch showing one second beside a wavy line with many small waves counted off.

terms.meaning: The unit for frequency. One hertz means one vibration each second. It is written Hz, and is named after the German scientist Heinrich Hertz.
terms.example: A string that vibrates 440 times a second has a frequency of 440 hertz.
terms.art: The words '440 vibrations in 1 second = 440 Hz' beside a vibrating string.

terms.meaning: A springy thing goes back to its shape after you bend, stretch or squeeze it. Scientists call this being elastic.
terms.example: A stretched string, a tight drum skin and squeezed air are all springy. That is why all three can vibrate.
terms.art: A rubber band, a balloon skin and a closed plastic bottle being squeezed, each with small arrows showing it pushing back.

terms.meaning: A thin length of wire, gut or thread, held tight at both ends. When it is plucked, bowed or struck, it vibrates.
terms.example: The veena, the sitar, the violin and the guitar are string instruments.
terms.art: A veena lying on a mat, with one string drawn as a blur.

terms.meaning: A thin sheet stretched tight over a frame. Scientists call it a membrane. When it is struck, the whole sheet vibrates.
terms.example: The heads of a mridangam, a tabla and a chenda are skins. So is your eardrum.
terms.art: A drum seen from the side with its skin drawn bulging slightly up and then slightly down.

terms.meaning: The air inside a tube or a pipe. This air can vibrate back and forth along the tube.
terms.example: In a bansuri, a nadaswaram or a bottle you blow across, the air column makes the note.
terms.art: A bansuri cut open along its length to show the air inside, with small arrows pointing back and forth along the tube.

terms.meaning: A thin strip of cane or metal that flaps quickly when air is blown past it. It starts the air column vibrating.
terms.example: A nadaswaram and a shehnai have reeds made of cane. A harmonium has metal reeds.
terms.art: A close-up of the cane reed at the top of a nadaswaram, with wavy lines beside it.

terms.meaning: A wide, thin surface joined to a string. The string makes it vibrate, and the wide surface pushes much more air than the thin string can.
terms.example: The hollow jackwood body of a veena is its soundboard. Without it you would hardly hear the string.
terms.art: A thin string pushing a few air particles, beside a wide wooden board pushing a large crowd of air particles.

terms.meaning: The material that a sound travels through. A medium can be a solid, a liquid or a gas.
terms.example: When someone calls you, the medium is air. For a whale's song, the medium is sea water.
terms.art: Three panels: sound lines crossing air, crossing water with a whale, and running along a steel rail.

terms.meaning: The tiny pieces that every material is made of. They are far too small to see. A sound travels when each particle pushes the next one.
terms.example: Air particles pass the push from a drum skin to your ear. Each particle moves only a tiny way and comes back.
terms.art: A row of dots, with one bunch of dots crowded together and an arrow showing the crowded place moving along the row.

terms.meaning: A thin skin about 9 millimetres across, at the inner end of the ear hole. Sound makes it vibrate.
terms.example: When a mridangam is played, your eardrum vibrates at the same frequency as the drum skin.
terms.art: A cut-away drawing of an ear with the eardrum shown as a small tight skin and three tiny bones behind it.

terms.meaning: Anything that takes the energy out of a vibration, so that it dies away. Touching, soft cloth and the air itself all damp a vibration.
terms.example: A sitar player rests a hand on the strings to stop them. That is damping.
terms.art: A hand pinching the rim of a ringing steel tumbler, with the wavy sound lines fading out.

terms.meaning: In a fair test, the one thing you change on purpose.
terms.example: In the Comb Test, the independent variable is the time the stroke takes.
terms.art: A notebook table with the first column circled and labelled 'what I change'.

terms.meaning: In a fair test, the thing you watch or measure to see what happens.
terms.example: In the Comb Test, the dependent variable is what you hear: ticks, a rattle, a buzz or a note.
terms.art: A notebook table with the last column circled and labelled 'what I measure'.

terms.meaning: In a fair test, the things you keep the same, so that only one thing changes.
terms.example: In the Comb Test, the comb, the card and the 40 teeth stay the same for every stroke.
terms.art: A comb, a card and a ruler in a row, each with a small 'same every time' tick mark.

explanations.definition: A vibration is a movement back and forth past a rest position, repeated again and again.
explanations.description: Every sound starts with something vibrating. To describe a vibration you need two numbers. The amplitude says how far the thing moves from its rest position. The frequency says how many full trips it makes each second. Frequency is measured in hertz. Most sound sources vibrate too quickly to watch. A plucked string looks like a blur because it passes the same places hundreds of times a second. The blur is widest where the string moves most. The two numbers are separate. Pluck harder and the amplitude grows, so the sound is louder, but the frequency stays the same. A young person can hear frequencies from about 20 hertz to about 20,000 hertz.
examples: In the Slow String, a chain of rubber bands with a peg on it swung about 3 times a second. That was slow enough to watch.
The lowest string of a guitar vibrates about 82 times a second.
A mosquito's wings beat several hundred times a second, which is why the whine is so high.
explanations.art: A string shown as a blur, with one arrow marking the amplitude from the middle line to the edge, and a stopwatch counting the trips in one second.

explanations.definition: A thing vibrates when it is springy and has weight. Its springiness pulls it back towards its rest position, and its own movement carries it past.
explanations.description: Pull a string to one side and let go. The tight string pulls itself back towards the middle. As it goes, it speeds up. It is moving fastest at the moment it reaches its rest position, so it cannot stop there. It carries on to the other side. Now the string is pulled back the other way. It slows, stops for an instant and returns. This repeats until the energy of the pluck is used up. Two things set the frequency. A stronger pull back gives a faster vibration. More weight to move gives a slower vibration. A shorter string also has less to move, so it vibrates faster. The same two rules work for a drum skin and for the air in a pipe.
examples: In the Slow String, a clothes peg clipped to the chain made it swing more slowly. There was more weight to move.
In the Slow String, stepping back to pull the chain tighter made it swing faster, until it was a blur.
The low strings of a guitar or a violin are wound with fine wire. The wire adds weight, so a tight string can still vibrate slowly.
explanations.art: Four small pictures of a string in a row: pulled up and still, passing the middle with a long speed arrow, pulled down and still, passing the middle again.

explanations.concept: How separate pushes become a note
explanations.definition: Each vibration gives the air one push. Above about 20 pushes a second, human ears stop hearing them one by one and hear a steady note.
explanations.description: In the Comb Test, each tooth bent the card and let it snap back. Each snap pushed the air once. At 5 or 10 pushes a second you heard every tick. At about 20 the ticks ran together into a rattle. At 80 you heard a low note. Nothing changed except how fast the pushes came. A higher frequency gives a higher note. The note of a string, a drum or a flute is made in the same way. The string pushes the air once in every vibration. So 440 vibrations a second send 440 pushes a second to your ear. In 1681 the English scientist Robert Hooke showed this with a toothed wheel. He held a card against the turning teeth. When the wheel turned faster, the note rose.
examples: A male cricket has a row of tiny teeth on one wing. He draws the edge of the other wing across it, as you drew the card across the comb.
A zip makes a rising 'zzzip' when you pull it faster.
A cat's purr is about 25 pushes a second. That is slow enough to feel each one with your hand.
explanations.art: A comb and a card at the top, and below it three rows of dots: far apart labelled 'ticks', closer labelled 'rattle', and crowded labelled 'note'.

explanations.definition: Most musical instruments make sound with one of three vibrating things: a tight string, a tight skin, or the air inside a tube.
explanations.description: A string is plucked, bowed or struck. Its note depends on its length, its tightness and its weight. A thin string moves very little air. So it is joined through a bridge to a soundboard or a hollow body. A skin is struck with a hand or a stick. Its note depends on its size, its tightness and its weight. The black patch on a tabla is a paste of rice flour and fine iron or stone powder. It adds weight in the middle of the skin. An air column is the air inside a tube. Something must start it: a reed, the player's lips, or a stream of breath across an edge. Air is springy and it has weight, so it vibrates back and forth along the tube. A longer column vibrates more slowly and gives a lower note.
examples: String instruments include the veena, the sitar, the sarod, the violin, the guitar, the tanpura and the ektara of the Bauls.
Instruments with skins include the mridangam, the tabla, the chenda, the parai, the dhol and the pung of Manipur.
Instruments with an air column include the bansuri, the nadaswaram, the shehnai, the conch and the trumpet. In the Palm Pipe, the air in a cardboard tube gave a note when you slapped the end.
explanations.art: Three instruments side by side, a veena, a mridangam and a bansuri, each with the vibrating part coloured: the string, the skin and the air inside.

explanations.concept: Your voice, and the voices of other animals
explanations.definition: A voice is made by two small folds in the voice box, called the vocal folds. Breath from the lungs blows them apart, and they spring shut again, many times a second.
explanations.description: The voice box is the bump you can feel at the front of your throat. Its proper name is the larynx. When you speak, the two folds open and close about 250 times a second in a child. That is about 200 times in a woman and about 120 times in a man. Each opening lets out one puff of air, and each puff is one push. The puffs then pass through the throat and the mouth, which are an air column. So a voice uses folds that act like a skin, and an air column that shapes the sound. Tighter, thinner folds vibrate faster and give a higher note. Humans are one animal among many who make sound this way. Cows, cats, dogs and frogs have vocal folds too. A bird sings with a different organ, deeper in the chest, called the syrinx. Insects mostly rub or beat hard parts of the body.
examples: In Sss and Zzz, your fingers felt a buzz on your throat for 'zzz' but not for 'sss'.
In Sss and Zzz, your hum stopped when you pinched your nose, because the breath could no longer flow.
A male cricket sings by rubbing his wings. A bee's hum is the beat of her wings.
explanations.art: A view down a throat showing two pale folds, drawn once open and once closed, with small puffs of air rising between them.

explanations.concept: How the vibration reaches your ear
explanations.definition: A vibration travels through a medium because each particle pushes the next. The sound reaches you when the pushes make your eardrum vibrate.
explanations.description: Air is made of particles with spaces between them. When a drum skin moves outwards, it squeezes the air particles next to it closer together. Those particles push the ones beyond them, and so on across the room. Each particle moves only a tiny way and then comes back. The squeeze travels, and the air stays where it was. The same thing happens in water and in a solid, where the particles are closer together. In the Spoon on a String, the vibration ran along the string to your fingers. From there it passed through the bones of your head. Sound travels at about 340 metres a second in air and about 1,500 in water. In steel it travels at about 5,000 metres a second. Where there are no particles, as in space, there is nothing to pass the push on. At the ear, the pushes make the eardrum vibrate. Three tiny bones pass the vibration to the inner ear, which is full of liquid. Nerves carry signals from there to the brain.
examples: In the Thali and the Skin, the sound of a steel plate crossed the air. It made grains jump on a skin that nothing touched.
In the Spoon on a String, the ring was louder and longer through the string than through the air.
A whale's song travels through sea water for many kilometres.
explanations.art: A drum on the left, a row of air particles with one crowded band moving to the right, and an ear on the right with the eardrum and three small bones.

explanations.definition: A vibration dies away because its energy leaves. Some energy goes into the air as sound, and the rest warms the vibrating thing and whatever touches it.
explanations.description: A pluck gives a string a fixed amount of energy. Every vibration passes a little of that energy to the air. The amplitude shrinks, the sound grows softer, and at last the string is still. Anything that takes the energy faster is called damping. A finger on a string takes the energy almost at once. A soundboard takes energy from the string quickly and gives it to the air. So an instrument with a soundboard is louder, but its note dies sooner. A hard table does the same for a buzzing phone. The phone hardly moves the air by itself, but the whole table top moves a great deal of air. A soft pad under the phone keeps the vibration out of the table.
examples: In the Blur and the Pinch, the tumbler stopped ringing the moment you pinched its rim.
In Quiet the Buzz, the phone was loud on a steel plate and much quieter on a folded towel.
A mixer-grinder stands on rubber feet, so that less of its vibration passes into the kitchen counter.
explanations.art: A plucked string whose blur gets thinner from left to right, with small arrows carrying energy away into the air and into a wooden board.

explanations.description: Vibration is found far beyond music. The particles of every solid vibrate all the time, millions of millions of times a second. That movement is what we call heat. A quartz crystal in a watch vibrates 32,768 times a second and keeps the time. After a very large earthquake the whole Earth rings for weeks. Its slowest vibration takes about 54 minutes. The surface of the Sun rises and falls about every five minutes. Some people go further and say that everything is vibration. Here the views differ.
examples: Heat in a steel tumbler is the vibration of its particles.
The Earth rang for weeks after the Sumatra earthquake of December 2004.
String theory describes every particle as a tiny vibrating string. No experiment has tested it yet.

perspectives.who: Physicists who use quantum field theory
perspectives.explanation: Our best tested theory describes every particle as a ripple in a field that fills all of space. An electron is a ripple in the electron field. This is a very exact way of calculating, and it has passed every test so far.

Every kind of particle may be one kind of tiny string, vibrating in different ways. One veena string gives different notes in the same way. The mathematics is promising. Nobody has yet found a way to test the idea by experiment.

perspectives.who: The musician and scholar Sharngadeva, about 800 years ago
perspectives.explanation: In the first chapter of his book on music, the Sangita Ratnakara, sound (nada) is treated as the root of music and, in a deeper sense, of all things. This is a teaching about meaning. It was not offered as a measurement.

A ripple in a field, the jiggling of particles and the swing of a string are different things. Calling them all 'vibration' uses one word for many ideas. The word should not be stretched until it explains nothing.

explanations.art: A veena string, a wristwatch with a small crystal drawn inside, the Earth with faint ripples round it, and the Sun, in a row from small to large.

agreed.text: Every sound source vibrates. When the vibration stops, the sound stops.
agreed.evidence: Touch any ringing thing and the sound ends as the movement ends. High-speed cameras show strings, drum skins and vocal folds moving back and forth.

agreed.text: The note we hear depends on the frequency, which is the number of vibrations each second.
agreed.evidence: In 1681 Robert Hooke held a card against a turning toothed wheel. When the wheel turned faster, the note rose. The Comb Test shows the same thing.

agreed.text: Sound needs a medium. It travels through solids, liquids and gases, and it cannot cross empty space.
agreed.evidence: About 1660, Robert Boyle and Robert Hooke pumped the air out of a glass jar with a bell inside. The bell still moved, but its sound grew much fainter.

agreed.text: A bigger vibration gives a louder sound, and it does not change the note.
agreed.evidence: A string plucked gently and the same string plucked hard give the same note. Only the width of the blur and the loudness change.

agreed.text: A vibration dies away because its energy passes into the air as sound and into the material as heat.
agreed.evidence: A string joined to a soundboard is louder and stops sooner than the same string held between two fingers. The energy of the pluck is spent faster.

challenging.claim: Sound is a stream of tiny particles thrown out by the thing that makes the sound.
challenging.who: The Greek thinker Epicurus and the Roman poet Lucretius, more than 2,000 years ago
challenging.for: A sound does seem to leave its source and arrive at the ear, as a thrown ball does. A louder sound could be more particles.
challenging.against: A bell inside a jar goes quiet when the air is pumped out, though the bell still moves. Thrown particles would cross the empty jar easily. So sound needs the air to carry it.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of what sound is: tiny particles thrown from the source to the ear.

challenging.claim: 'Sound travels best through solids' is only half the story.
challenging.for: Sound is faster in a solid, and a string or a rail keeps it from spreading out. That is why the spoon rang so loudly through the string. But sound in the air hardly gets into a solid or a liquid at all. Almost all of it bounces off the surface. That is why a shut window keeps out street noise.
challenging.against: Many school books say only that solids carry sound best, then liquids, then gases. That is true once the vibration is inside the material.
challenging.context: This card is about a line found in many school books: that solids carry sound better than liquids and gases.

challenging.claim: Vibrations slower than 20 a second are not sound.
challenging.who: A common line in school books
challenging.for: Human ears hear nothing below about 20 vibrations a second, however strong the vibration is.
challenging.against: Elephants and pigeons hear vibrations slower than that. The air does the same thing at 15 vibrations a second as at 50. Scientists call these slow vibrations infrasound. Whether to call them 'sound' depends on who is listening.
challenging.context: This card is about very slow vibrations, which humans cannot hear but some other animals can.

challenging.who: Plant scientists such as Heidi Appel, Rex Cocroft and Lilach Hadany
challenging.for: Plants sense vibrations and act on them. In a 2014 study, thale cress plants made more defence chemicals after feeling the vibrations of a caterpillar chewing. In a 2019 study, evening primrose flowers made sweeter nectar within three minutes of the sound of a flying bee.
challenging.against: Some scientists say that responding to a vibration is not the same as hearing. They want the studies repeated by other teams. Claims that music makes plants grow better rest on weak tests.
challenging.context: This card is about whether plants sense sound. A sound is a vibration, and a leaf or a flower can be shaken by it.

challenging.claim: Everything in the universe is made of tiny vibrating strings.
challenging.for: In the mathematics, one kind of string vibrating in different ways could give every known particle, and gravity too.
challenging.against: After fifty years there is still no experiment that can test it. Many physicists say an idea that cannot be tested is not yet science.
challenging.context: This card is about string theory, an untested idea in physics. It uses the picture of a vibrating string for the smallest things there are.

big_questions.q: In the Comb Test, 40 ticks became one note. Did the ticks join together in the air, or in you?
big_questions.hint: A microphone would still record 40 separate pushes. Think about what your ear and brain add.

big_questions.q: A plucked string is moving fastest as it passes its rest position. So how does a vibrating thing ever come to rest?
big_questions.hint: Think about the Slow String. Did each swing go as far as the one before?

big_questions.q: An elephant hears vibrations too slow for you. A bat hears vibrations too fast for you. Whose list of sounds is the right one?
big_questions.hint: Is there one list of sounds in the world, or one list for each kind of ear?

big_questions.q: When a string stops vibrating, where has the energy of your pluck gone?
big_questions.hint: Some went into the air as sound. Where does sound go when it fades?

big_questions.q: Atoms, the Earth and the Sun all vibrate. Does that make the universe a kind of music, or is that only a way of speaking?
big_questions.hint: What would have to be true for it to be music? Does music need a listener?

story.title: The String with a Coat
story.note: Tresa, Lilly Ammayi and Joby are made up, and so is the shop. 'Ammayi' is a Malayalam word for aunt. These things are real: Fort Kochi is a harbour town in Kerala. The low strings of guitars, violins and pianos are a thin core string with fine wire wound round it. The wire adds weight, so the string vibrates slowly while staying tight. A springy plank bounces more slowly under a heavy load than under a light one. Winding a string by hand with a drill is possible, but it is slow and the result is rough. String makers use a winding machine.
text: The last ferry had already gone when Joby came to the shop. Rain was falling hard on Fort Kochi, and the sea was the colour of a steel plate.

Tresa was ten. Every evening after school she helped her aunt, Lilly Ammayi, who mended instruments in a narrow shop behind the fish market. Violins hung from the ceiling. A harmonium lay open on the bench with its metal reeds in a row.
Joby was twelve, and he was soaked. He carried a guitar wrapped in a plastic sheet.
"It was my grandfather's," he said. "I am playing at the church feast tomorrow evening. Look."
The thickest string had snapped. It hung from the guitar in two curls.

Ammayi looked through her tin of strings. "Only thin ones," she said. "The thick ones come from Ernakulam, and no boat will cross tonight." She turned to Tresa. "You have until tomorrow noon. I have a harmonium to finish."
Then she went back to her bench. That was how Ammayi taught. She gave you the problem, and then she gave you room.
Tresa fitted a thin string where the thick one had been. She tightened it and plucked. The note was clear, and far too high.
"Loosen it," said Joby. "Loose strings sound lower."

He was right. She turned the peg back, and the note slid down, lower and lower. But the string grew slack. By the time the note was low enough, the string flopped against the wood and rattled. It hardly made a sound at all.
"Too loose to play," said Joby. "So a low string has to be a thick string. And we have no thick string."

Tresa went to the door to think. The rain had thinned. Down at the jetty, a plank lay from the stone edge to a fishing boat. A grey cat ran across, and the plank shivered quickly under her feet. Then a woman crossed with a full crate of sardines on her head. Under her, the same plank dipped and rose slowly, once for each step.
Tresa watched until the woman reached the boat.
It was the same plank, and just as springy as before. Only the weight on it had changed. With more weight to move, it bounced more slowly.

She ran back inside and picked up the two curls of the broken string. She had always taken it for one fat wire. Now she held the broken end under the lamp and bent it. Something was coming undone. A wire as fine as a hair was unwinding, round and round, from a plain thin string in the middle.
"Joby," she said. "It was never a thick string. It is a thin string wearing a coat."
"Why would a string need a coat?"

"To be heavy. A heavy string moves slowly, even when it is pulled tight. The string must be tight so that it rings. It must be heavy so that it moves slowly. And a string that moves slowly gives a low note."
Ammayi did not look up from the harmonium. "There is copper wire in the dead fan motor under the bench," she said.

It took them until late. They gripped one end of a thin string in the hand drill and tied the other end to the vice. Joby turned the handle slowly. Tresa fed the copper wire on, each turn tight against the last, like thread on a bobbin. Twice the coat came loose, and twice they began again.
At last she fitted the string to the guitar and turned the peg. The string tightened. She plucked it.
The note was low and steady, and it went on ringing. It was not quite the old sound. It was a little dull, as a first try often is. Joby played the first line of the feast hymn, and grinned.
Ammayi came over then. She plucked the string once and listened until it faded.
"Tomorrow," she said, "you can tell me why the thin strings wear no coat."
Tresa was already working it out.
story.epiphany: For the parent: how fast a string vibrates depends on two things. One is how hard it is pulled back, which is its tightness. The other is how much there is to move, which is its weight. Loosening a thin string lowers the note, but leaves the string too slack to ring. Winding wire round the string adds weight without loosening it. So the string vibrates slowly and still rings. Tresa saw the same rule in the plank, which bounced slowly under a heavy load.
ask: A loose string gave a low note. So why could Joby not just play on the loose string?
The plank was the same under the cat and under the woman. What changed, and what did that do to the bounce?
Why do the thin, high strings of a guitar need no wire wound round them?
Tresa's string sounded a little dull. What might be different between her winding and one made by a machine?

roots.context: In this unit you turned separate ticks into a note, and watched a slow string pass its rest position. Here we ask what a note really is, and who makes it.

deep_truth.truth: In the Comb Test, a slow stroke over 40 teeth gave 40 separate ticks. A quick stroke over the same teeth gave one steady note. Only the speed had changed. So a steady note is a row of separate pushes, arriving too quickly for the ear to hear apart.
deep_truth.habit: We treat a tick and a note as two kinds of sound, one broken and one smooth. They are the same kind at different speeds. The pushes stay separate in the air. Above about 20 pushes a second, a human ear reports them as one note.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Comb Test, 5 and 10 ticks a second were heard one by one. About 20 gave a rattle, and 80 gave a low note. Robert Hooke's toothed wheel showed the same in 1681. A male cricket makes his song by drawing a scraper across a row of teeth on his wing.

three.who_am_i: Your voice is your own body vibrating. Two small folds in your throat open and close about 250 times a second when you speak.
three.what_is_life: Living beings make and catch vibrations all day. A male cricket draws one wing across the other. A spider reads her web through her feet. You do it with a throat and two eardrums.
three.what_is_this_world: Anything that is springy and has weight can vibrate: a string, the air, the ground, the Sun. The world goes on ringing for a while after every push.

roots.thread: In the Comb Test, 40 separate ticks became one note. Looked at closely, the one note is still many pushes. So 'one' and 'many' can be two true descriptions of the same event. Which one you get depends on how fast the pushes come, and on who is listening. Many sages taught that the many different things in the world are really one thing, which we meet only a part at a time. The Comb Test does not prove that. It does show, with a comb and a card, how many can be heard as one.

teachings.source: Zhuangzi, chapter 2, 'On Making Things Equal' (China, about 2,300 years ago)
teachings.teaching: A teacher describes the wind blowing through all the hollows of a forest. Each hollow gives its own sound: some roar, some whistle, some sigh. Then he asks who does the sounding.
teachings.link: This is an air column, described long ago. In the Palm Pipe, a long tube and a short tube gave different notes from the same slap. Each hollow gives the note that its own length sets. The book leaves its question open, and so do we.
verse: 夫大塊噫氣，其名爲風。是唯无作，作則萬竅怒呺。
夫吹萬不同而使其自己也，咸其自取，怒者其誰邪？

teachings.teaching: This book on music speaks of two kinds of sound. The struck sound is made when things meet, and it is the sound of all music. The unstruck sound is said to be heard only in deep stillness.
teachings.link: Every sound in this unit is a struck sound. Something was plucked, hit, rubbed or blown, and then it vibrated. Science studies this kind. The unstruck sound is a teaching about the mind, and science does not measure it.

teachings.source: Aristotle, On the Soul, book 2, chapter 8 (Greece, about 2,350 years ago)
teachings.teaching: A sound needs three things: something that strikes, something that is struck, and a medium between them and the ear. The air must be moved as one mass, all the way to the hearing.
teachings.link: This matches the chain you built in the Spoon on a String: a source, a medium and an ear. Aristotle did not know about particles, but he saw that the air must carry the movement.
verse: Γίνεται δ’ ὁ κατ’ ἐνέργειαν ψόφος ἀεί τινος πρός τι καὶ ἔν τινι· πληγὴ γάρ ἐστιν ἡ ποιοῦσα.
ἕτερον γὰρ τὸ τύπτον καὶ τὸ τυπτόμενον
Ψοφητικὸν μὲν οὖν τὸ κινητικὸν ἑνὸς ἀέρος συνεχείᾳ μέχρις ἀκοῆς

science.text: The particles of every solid vibrate all the time. This movement is what we measure as temperature. It never stops completely, even at the lowest temperature there can be.
Our best tested theory, quantum field theory, describes every particle as a ripple in a field that fills space.
String theory says every particle is a tiny vibrating string. No experiment has tested it.

other_view.who: Many physicists, and people who study hearing
other_view.view: The ticks of the comb blend because of how human ears and brains work. That is a fact about ears, and it says little about the world. Vibration itself is ordinary. Anything that is pushed from rest and pulled back will vibrate, and forces and weight explain it fully. On this view, calling the world 'a vibration' borrows a word from music and stretches it too far.

practice.title: The bee hum
practice.say: Sit up and close your lips. Breathe in, then hum one long, low note, like a bee. Rest your fingertips on your throat, then on your cheeks, then on the top of your head. Notice where you feel the hum most. Now stop humming and sit quite still. Notice the moment when the buzz in your body fades. Do this three times.
practice.kid: Close your lips and hum like a bee. Touch your throat, your cheeks and your head. Where is the buzz strongest? Stop, and feel the buzz fade. Do it three times.

ask: In the Comb Test, 40 ticks became one note. Was the note made by the comb, by the air, or by your ear?
Elephants and pigeons hear vibrations too slow for you to hear. Is a sound still a sound when you cannot hear it?
When the plucked string is still again, where is your pluck now?
roots.art: A child sitting cross-legged with eyes closed and fingertips on her throat, humming, with a row of small dots leaving her lips that crowd together into one smooth line.

games.title: Tighter, Heavier, Shorter: what happens to the vibration?
games.context: This is a card game about what makes a vibration faster or slower. Each card describes one change to a string, a skin or an air column. You say whether the vibration becomes faster, slower or stays the same.

printables.title: 20 change cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: A veena player turns a peg and makes a string tighter.
items.b: FASTER. A tighter string is pulled back harder.

items.f: A guitar string is loosened by turning its peg back.
items.b: SLOWER. A looser string is pulled back less hard.

items.f: A sitar player presses a string onto a fret, so a shorter part vibrates.
items.b: FASTER. A shorter string has less to move.

items.f: Fine wire is wound round a string, and it is pulled just as tight as before.
items.b: SLOWER. The wire adds weight to move.

items.f: A tabla player taps the rim with a small hammer to tighten the skin.
items.b: FASTER. A tighter skin is pulled back harder.

items.f: A paste of wet rava is pressed onto the middle of a mridangam skin.
items.b: SLOWER. The paste adds weight to move.

items.f: On a damp monsoon day, a drum skin goes slack.
items.b: SLOWER. A slack skin is pulled back less hard.

items.f: A parai drum is warmed near a fire, and its skin tightens.
items.b: FASTER. A tighter skin is pulled back harder.

items.f: A bansuri player covers more holes, so the air column is longer.
items.b: SLOWER. A longer air column has more air to move.

items.f: A bansuri player lifts her fingers, so the air column is shorter.
items.b: FASTER. A shorter air column has less air to move.

items.f: Water is poured into a bottle, and you blow across the top.
items.b: FASTER. The air column above the water is now shorter.

items.f: A bell maker casts a bigger bell from the same metal.
items.b: SLOWER. A bigger bell has more metal to move.

items.f: A child grows up, and the vocal folds grow longer and thicker.
items.b: SLOWER. Bigger folds have more to move, so the voice is lower.

items.f: A singer stretches her vocal folds tighter.
items.b: FASTER. Tighter folds are pulled back harder.

items.f: A clothes peg is clipped to the middle of a string made of rubber bands.
items.b: SLOWER. The peg adds weight to move.

items.f: A string is changed for a heavier one, pulled just as tight.
items.b: SLOWER. A heavier string has more to move.

items.f: You pluck the same string much harder.
items.b: THE SAME. The amplitude is bigger and the sound is louder, but the frequency does not change.

items.f: You strike the same drum more gently.
items.b: THE SAME. The amplitude is smaller and the sound is softer, but the frequency does not change.

items.f: A steel tumbler is tapped empty, then filled with water and tapped again.
items.b: SLOWER. The water adds weight for the walls of the tumbler to move.

items.f: A cardboard tube is cut to half its length, and you slap the end.
items.b: FASTER. A shorter air column has less air to move.

rules: Shuffle the 20 cards into a pile, change side up. Each player takes three vote tokens: FASTER, SLOWER and THE SAME.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the change aloud, keeping the back hidden.
Every other player puts one vote token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader reads the back. Each player with the right vote scores 1 point.
A player who also gave the right reason scores 1 more point. The reasons are: pulled back harder, more to move, or less to move.
With two players, swap the reader after every card. The reader does not vote on their own card.
Playing alone? Read a card, say your vote and your reason aloud, then turn the card over. Score 1 point for each right vote.
After all 20 cards, the player with the most points wins. If you play alone, your score out of 20 is your result.

setup.art: Twenty cards in a pile on a table, and three small tokens marked FASTER, SLOWER and THE SAME in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while two others each slide one token forward, face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads the change. Everyone else votes with a token, face down.

setup.art: The tokens turned face up, and the reader showing the back of the card.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. The reader reads the answer and the reason.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 20 cards and three tokens for each player. 2. Shuffle the cards into a pile, change side up. 3. Choose the first reader.
flow.say: Each card changes one thing about a string, a skin or an air column. We vote on whether it will vibrate faster, slower or the same.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards. Choose who reads first.
flow.context: This is the first step of Tighter, Heavier, Shorter. You set out the change cards and the vote tokens.

flow.do: 1. The reader reads the top card. 2. The others vote with a token, face down, then turn the tokens over. 3. The reader reads the back. 4. Give 1 point for a right vote and 1 more for the right reason.
flow.say: Before you vote, ask yourself two things. Is it pulled back harder or less hard? Is there more to move or less?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Vote faster, slower or the same. Say your reason. Then check the back.

ask.q: Plucking a string harder does not change how fast it vibrates. What does it change?
good: The amplitude. The string moves farther away from its rest position.
The loudness.

flow.parent: Two cards have the answer THE SAME. They catch a common mix-up between loudness and the height of a note.
flow.context: This is the main part of Tighter, Heavier, Shorter. You vote on each change card and give a reason.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Sort the cards into three heaps by their reason: pulled back harder or less hard, more or less to move, and no change. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Let us sort the cards by reason. Which heap is biggest? Can you think of a change that is not on any card?
flow.kid: Count the points. Sort the cards by their reason. Which heap is biggest?

check.q: Which change makes a drum skin vibrate more slowly?
options: Sticking a lump of paste on it
Tightening it
Hitting it harder
check.why: The paste adds weight, so there is more to move and the skin vibrates more slowly. Tightening makes it faster. Hitting harder makes it louder, and leaves the frequency the same.

flow.context: This is the last step of Tighter, Heavier, Shorter. You sort the change cards by the reason on the back.

games.title: Pass It On: build the chain from the source to the ear
games.context: This is a card game about how a vibration travels. Each card is one link in a chain that starts at a sound source. You lay the links in the right order.

printables.title: 25 link cards to cut out (the chain and the place in it are on the back)

items.f: A finger plucks the veena string.
items.b: Chain A (Veena), link 1 of 5

items.f: The veena string vibrates.
items.b: Chain A (Veena), link 2 of 5

items.f: The bridge passes the vibration to the hollow wooden body of the veena.
items.b: Chain A (Veena), link 3 of 5

items.f: The wide body of the veena vibrates and pushes the air around it.

items.b: Chain D (Whale), link 2 of 5

items.b: Chain D (Whale), link 4 of 5

items.f: The ear bones of a second whale, far away, pick up the vibration.
items.b: Chain D (Whale), link 5 of 5

items.f: A wooden spoon strikes the steel thali.
items.b: Chain E (Thali), link 1 of 5

items.f: The thali vibrates.
items.b: Chain E (Thali), link 2 of 5

items.b: Chain E (Thali), link 3 of 5

items.f: The cling-film skin on the bowl vibrates.
items.b: Chain E (Thali), link 4 of 5

items.f: The grains of rava on the skin jump.
items.b: Chain E (Thali), link 5 of 5

rules: There are five chains of five links: the veena, the bansuri, the spoon on a string, the whale and the thali.
Shuffle the 25 cards and deal them all out, link side up. With two players, deal 12 each and put the last card to one side. Either player may lay it when it fits.
On your turn, lay one card on the table. A card may be laid only in two cases. It is the first link of a chain, or it is the next link after a card already there.
Say aloud what passes the vibration on to what. For example: 'The string passes it to the bridge.'
If you cannot lay a card, you miss your turn.
Any player may ask for a check. Turn the card over and read its place. A card in the wrong place goes back to its owner.
The first player to lay all their cards wins. Play on until all five chains are complete.
Playing alone? Shuffle the cards and build all five chains. Then turn the cards over to check. Your score is the number in the right place, out of 25.

setup.art: Twenty-five small cards spread on a floor mat, each with one sentence on it.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 25 link cards. Shuffle them and deal them out.

setup.art: Two chains of cards growing in rows on the mat, one beginning 'A finger plucks the veena string'.
setup.caption: 2. Lay a first link, or the next link of a chain on the table.

setup.art: A child turning over a row of five cards to show 'Chain A, link 1' to 'Chain A, link 5' in order.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the cards over to check the order.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 25 cards. 2. Read out the names of the five chains. 3. Shuffle the cards and deal them out, link side up.
flow.say: Every sound reaches a listener through a chain. Something vibrates, something carries the vibration, and something receives it. Let us build five chains.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. Deal them out with the words facing up.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pass It On. You deal out the link cards for five chains.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to lay one card. 2. A card must be a first link, or the next link of a chain already on the table. 3. Each player says what passes the vibration to what.
flow.say: Which card starts a chain? Look for the pluck, the breath, the tap or the strike. What does that first thing make vibrate?
flow.kid: Lay a first link or a next link. Say what passes the vibration on.

ask.q: Which chains pass through a gas, which through a liquid and which through a solid?
good: The veena, the bansuri and the thali go through air, a gas.
The whale's song goes through sea water, a liquid.
The spoon's ring goes along a string, a solid.

flow.parent: If a player is stuck, ask what is touching the vibrating thing. The vibration can only pass to something that touches it.
flow.context: This is the main part of Pass It On. You take turns to lay the link cards in order, from the source to the listener.

flow.do: 1. Turn each chain over to check the order. 2. Ask what every chain has in common. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Look at all five chains. What does every chain start with? What does every chain need in the middle?
flow.kid: Turn the cards over to check. What does every chain start with?

check.q: What does every sound need between the source and the listener?
options: A medium made of particles
A string
Empty space
check.why: A vibration is passed from particle to particle. So there must be a solid, a liquid or a gas in between. A string is only one kind of medium. Empty space has no particles, so it cannot carry a sound.

flow.context: This is the last step of Pass It On. You check the five chains and find what they all share.

experiments.title: The Comb Test: when do ticks become a note?
experiments.context: In this experiment you draw a card along 40 teeth of a comb, slowly and then faster. You find out how many ticks a second it takes before the ticks sound like one note.
experiments.question: How many ticks a second does it take before separate ticks sound like one steady note? What happens to the note when the ticks come faster still?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You will draw a card along 40 teeth of a comb in 8 seconds. Then you will do it in 4, 2, 1 and half a second. Which strokes will sound like separate ticks, and which like a note? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same comb, the same 40 teeth and the same card for every stroke. Press just as lightly each time. Change only one thing: the time the stroke takes. That time is the independent variable. What you hear is the dependent variable. Do every stroke three times, because a hand cannot keep a perfectly steady speed.
results_table: What we heard: ticks, rattle, buzz or note

materials.item: a plastic comb with at least 40 teeth of the same size
a stiff card about 5 cm by 8 cm, such as an old visiting card or a playing card
a sketch pen or a dab of nail polish, to mark two teeth
a phone stopwatch, or a clock with a seconds hand
a notebook page and a pencil

experiments.record: Draw a table with five rows, one for each stroke time: 8 seconds, 4 seconds, 2 seconds, 1 second and half a second. For each row, write the ticks each second and what you heard. Then write what you thought would happen, what you found, and why you think it happened.

schedule.what: Mark 40 teeth on a comb. Draw a card along them in 8, 4, 2, 1 and half a second. Write down what you hear each time.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
example_chart.note: These results are made up, to show what a finished table can look like. Write down what you really hear.

setup.art: A plastic comb held with its teeth pointing up, with a dot of red ink on one tooth and another dot on the fortieth tooth along.
setup.caption: 1. Count 40 teeth. Mark the first and the fortieth.

setup.art: A hand holding a stiff card upright so that its bottom edge rests between the teeth of a comb held in the other hand.
setup.caption: 2. Rest the edge of the card between the teeth at the first mark.

setup.art: The card being drawn along the comb while a grown-up watches a phone stopwatch.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the card to the second mark in the time you have chosen.

setup.art: A notebook table with three columns: the stroke time, the ticks each second and what was heard.
setup.caption: 4. Work out the ticks each second. Write down what you heard.

flow.do: 1. Count 40 teeth along the comb. 2. Mark the first tooth and the fortieth with the sketch pen. 3. Hold the comb in one hand with the teeth pointing up. 4. Rest the short edge of the card between the teeth, about 3 millimetres deep.
flow.say: We are going to draw this card along exactly 40 teeth. Each tooth will bend the card and let it snap back. So one stroke gives 40 ticks.
flow.kid: Count 40 teeth on the comb. Mark the first and the last. Rest the edge of the card between the teeth.
flow.parent: If the comb has fine teeth at one end and wide teeth at the other, mark 40 of one kind. Keep the other kind for a later step. A thin, bendy card gives a weak sound. A visiting card or a playing card works well.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Comb Test. You mark 40 teeth on a comb, so that every stroke of the card gives 40 ticks.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child the five stroke times: 8 seconds, 4 seconds, 2 seconds, 1 second and half a second. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason. 3. Write both down.
flow.say: A slow stroke will take 8 seconds, and the fastest will take half a second. Which strokes will sound like separate ticks? Which will sound like a note? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The slowest stroke takes 8 seconds. The fastest takes half a second. Which will give ticks? Which will give a note? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: A fast stroke makes the ticks come too close together to hear apart.
A zip makes a note when you pull it fast.
I think it will always be ticks, only quicker.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This step of the Comb Test is for guessing. You guess which strokes of the card will give ticks and which will give a note.

flow.do: 1. One person watches the stopwatch and counts the seconds aloud. 2. The other draws the card from the first mark to the second in 8 seconds. 3. Do it three times. 4. Then do the same in 4 seconds, three times. 5. Write what you heard, and work out 40 ÷ 8 and 40 ÷ 4.
flow.say: I will count the seconds aloud. Move the card steadily, so that you reach the second mark as I say eight. What do you hear? Can you count the ticks?
flow.kid: Draw the card along the 40 teeth in 8 seconds. Listen. Then do it in 4 seconds. Write what you hear.
flow.parent: 40 teeth in 8 seconds is 5 ticks each second. 40 teeth in 4 seconds is 10 ticks each second. Most people hear every tick at both speeds. The first tries are often jerky. That is why each stroke is done three times.
flow.context: In this step of the Comb Test you make two slow strokes, of 8 seconds and of 4 seconds. You listen for separate ticks.

flow.do: 1. Draw the card along the 40 teeth in 2 seconds, three times. 2. Then in 1 second, three times. 3. Then in half a second, three times. 4. After each one, write what you heard. 5. Work out 40 ÷ 2, 40 ÷ 1 and 40 ÷ a half.
flow.say: Now faster. Two seconds first, then one second, then half a second. Half a second is about as long as saying the word 'one'. Listen each time. Is it ticks, a rattle, a buzz or a note?
flow.kid: Now do it in 2 seconds. Then 1 second. Then half a second. Is it ticks, a rattle, a buzz or a note?

check.q: In the Comb Test, the card crosses 40 teeth in half a second. How many ticks is that each second?
check.why: In half a second there are 40 ticks. So in a whole second there would be twice as many, which is 80. If you chose 20, you halved the number. A shorter time means more ticks each second, so you double it.

flow.parent: The numbers are 20, 40 and 80 ticks each second. Half a second cannot be timed exactly by hand, and it does not need to be. One quick, smooth stroke is enough.
flow.context: In this step of the Comb Test you make three faster strokes: 2 seconds, 1 second and half a second. You listen for the ticks to turn into a note.

flow.do: 1. If the comb has wide teeth and fine teeth, stroke 5 centimetres of each kind in one second. 2. If it has one kind only, stroke 20 teeth in one second, and then 40 teeth in one second. 3. Ask which sounded higher.
flow.say: Here is one more test. Keep the stroke time at one second, and change the number of teeth the card crosses. Which gives the higher note? Why do you think that is?
flow.kid: Keep the time at 1 second. Cross few teeth, then many teeth. Which note is higher?

ask.q: Which gave the higher note, and why?
good: The one with more teeth, because more ticks reached my ear each second.
The fine teeth, because they are closer together.

flow.parent: More teeth in the same time means more ticks each second, and a higher note. This shows that the number of ticks each second sets the note.
flow.context: In this step of the Comb Test you keep the stroke time the same and change the number of teeth. It checks whether the number of ticks each second sets the note.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they heard, and why they think it happened. 3. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your table. Say what you thought would happen, what you heard, and why you think it happened. At about how many ticks a second did the ticks turn into a note?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you heard. Say why you think it happened.

ask.q: What was the only thing that changed between the ticks and the note?
good: The time the stroke took.
How many ticks came each second.
The comb, the card and the teeth were the same.

ask.q: A plucked string gives a note. What does that tell you about how the string is moving?
good: It must be pushing the air many times each second.
It moves back and forth too fast to see, like fast ticks.

flow.parent: Most people hear separate ticks at 5 and 10 a second, and a rattle at about 20. At about 40 they hear a rough buzz, and at 80 a low note. Your results may differ a little. The reason: each tooth bends the card and lets it snap back, so each tooth gives the air one push. Above about 20 pushes a second, human ears stop hearing the pushes one by one. We hear how fast they come, as a note. More pushes each second give a higher note. Robert Hooke showed this in London in 1681, with a card held against a turning toothed wheel.
flow.think: A mosquito's wings beat several hundred times a second. What does the comb tell you about the mosquito's whine?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Comb Test. You say what your table shows about ticks and notes.

experiments.title: The Thali and the Skin: how far can a sound shake a skin?
experiments.context: In this experiment you stretch cling film over a bowl to make a skin. You put a pinch of rava on it and strike a steel plate at different distances. You find out whether the sound can make the grains jump without touching them.
experiments.question: Can the sound of a steel plate make grains jump on a skin that nothing touches? From how far away?
experiments.predict: Guess first. A steel plate will be struck 10, 20, 40 and 80 centimetres from the skin. At which distances will the grains jump? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same plate and the same spoon. The same person strikes it each time, as nearly the same way as they can. Keep the grains and the skin the same. Change only the distance, which is the independent variable. The movement of the grains is the dependent variable. Do three strikes at each distance. Also swing the spoon once without hitting the plate. This checks that moving air from the swing is not what shakes the grains.
results_table: Distance from the plate to the bowl

materials.item: a steel bowl or a wide steel tumbler, 10 to 15 cm across
cling film, or a thin plastic carry bag cut open, or a large balloon cut open
materials.qty: one piece bigger than the bowl

materials.item: a strong rubber band that fits round the bowl
rava (sooji), or fine salt or sugar
a steel plate (thali) and a wooden spoon or ladle
a ruler or a measuring tape

experiments.safety: The clang of the plate is loud. The person who watches the grains covers both ears with their hands. Never strike the plate close to anyone's head.
experiments.record: Draw a table with one row for each distance: 10 cm, 20 cm, 40 cm and 80 cm. Give each strike a score: 2 if the grains jump or slide, 1 if they only tremble, 0 if they stay still. Add the three scores for each distance.

schedule.what: Make a skin of cling film on a bowl and put rava on it. Strike a steel plate at four distances. Score how much the grains move.

example_chart.note: These results are made up, to show what a finished table can look like. Write down what you really see.
