setup.art: A wooden spoon striking the middle of the plate while a child on the far side covers her ears and watches the grains jump.
setup.caption: 3. Strike the plate. Watch the grains. Give a score of 2, 1 or 0.

setup.art: The plate held 80 cm from the bowl, with a measuring tape laid along the table.
setup.caption: 4. Repeat at 20 cm, 40 cm and 80 cm, three strikes each.

flow.do: 1. Stretch the cling film over the bowl and hold it with the rubber band. 2. Pull the edges until the film is tight and smooth. 3. Put a small pinch of rava in the middle. 4. Stand the bowl on a table.
flow.say: This film is our skin. It is a thin sheet stretched tight, like the head of a drum. Tap it gently with one finger. What do the grains do?
flow.kid: Stretch the film tight over the bowl. Put a pinch of rava in the middle. Tap the film gently.
flow.parent: The film must be tight, with no wrinkles. A slack film hardly moves. About 20 to 30 grains are enough. A heap of grains is too heavy to jump.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Thali and the Skin. You make a tight skin of cling film on a bowl and put grains of rava on it.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the steel plate and the spoon. 2. Say that the plate will be struck in the air, touching nothing. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: I will hold this plate in the air and strike it. It will not touch the bowl or the table. Will the grains move? From how far away? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The plate will not touch the bowl. Will the grains move anyway? From how far? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: Sound is a vibration, so it might shake the film.
Nothing touches the bowl, so the grains will stay still.
It will work close by, because the sound is stronger there.

flow.context: This step of the Thali and the Skin is for guessing. You guess whether the sound of a struck plate can move grains without touching them.

flow.do: 1. The watcher covers both ears and looks at the grains from the far side. 2. Hold the plate upright by its rim, 10 cm from the bowl, with its flat face towards the bowl. 3. First swing the spoon and stop just before the plate. 4. Then strike the middle of the plate three times, with a pause between strikes. 5. Write a score for each strike.
flow.say: Cover your ears and watch the grains. First I will swing and not hit. Did the grains move? Now I will strike. Give each strike a score of 2, 1 or 0.
flow.kid: Cover your ears. Watch the grains. First a swing with no hit. Then three real strikes. Score each one.

check.q: In the Thali and the Skin, why swing the spoon once without hitting the plate?
options: To check that wind from the swing moves nothing
To warm up the arm
To make the plate ring longer
check.why: Suppose the grains stay still for a swing with no strike. Then the sound moved them, and the moving air did not. If you chose another answer, remember that a fair test rules out other causes.

flow.parent: At 10 cm, most of the grains should jump or slide when the plate is struck. If nothing moves, tighten the film, use fewer grains and strike harder.
flow.context: In this step of the Thali and the Skin the plate is struck 10 centimetres from the bowl. A swing with no strike comes first, as a check.

flow.do: 1. Measure 20 cm from the bowl and strike the plate three times there. 2. Do the same at 40 cm and at 80 cm. 3. Strike as nearly the same way as you can each time. 4. Write a score for every strike and add up each row.
flow.say: Now I will move back. I will try to strike just as hard each time. Why does that matter? Tell me the score after each strike.
flow.kid: Now the plate moves back. Score each strike at 20, 40 and 80 centimetres. Add up each row.
flow.parent: A hand cannot strike exactly the same way twice. Three strikes at each distance make one odd strike matter less. Expect the scores to fall as the plate moves away.
flow.context: In this step of the Thali and the Skin the plate is struck further from the bowl: 20, 40 and 80 centimetres. There are three strikes at each distance.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. 3. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your scores. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Nothing touched the bowl. So what carried the shake from the plate to the skin?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why you think it happened.

ask.q: What was between the plate and the skin?
good: Only air.
Air particles, which passed the pushes along.

ask.q: Which part of your own body is a small tight skin that sound shakes?
good: My eardrum.

flow.parent: The struck plate vibrates. Each vibration pushes the air next to the plate. The air particles pass the pushes on to the film, and the film vibrates and throws the grains up. Further away, the sound has spread out, so each push on the film is weaker. Your eardrum is a skin like this one, about 9 millimetres across. Sound makes it vibrate in the same way.
flow.think: The grains needed a loud clang. Your eardrum picks up a whisper. What does that tell you about how little the eardrum needs to move?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Thali and the Skin. You say what your scores show about how a sound crosses the air.

experiments.title: The Spoon on a String: does the ring travel better through air or through a solid?
experiments.context: In this experiment you hang a steel spoon on a string and tap it. You listen to the ring through the air, then through the string with your fingers at your ears. Then you try wool, rubber bands and water.
experiments.question: A tapped spoon rings. Does the ring reach your ears better through the air or along a string? Does the kind of string matter?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You will hear the same tapped spoon through the air and through cotton string. Then you will hear it through wool and through a chain of rubber bands. Which will carry the ring for the longest time? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same spoon, tapped by the same person in the same gentle way. Keep every string the same length, about 1 metre. Change only what the vibration travels through. That is the independent variable. Count the seconds you can hear the ring. That count is the dependent variable. Do three taps for each one.

materials.item: a steel tablespoon, and a second spoon to tap it with
cotton string, kite thread or twine, about 1 metre long
knitting wool, about 1 metre long
rubber bands, looped together into a chain about 1 metre long when gently pulled
a plastic bucket or a large steel vessel, half full of water

experiments.safety: Press your fingertips gently against the small flaps at the front of your ear holes. Do not push fingers or string inside the ears.
experiments.record: Draw a table with a row for each path: air, cotton string, wool and rubber bands. Write the seconds you heard the ring for each tap, and one or two words for how it sounded.

schedule.what: Hang a spoon on a string and tap it. Count how long you hear the ring through air, string, wool and rubber bands. Then listen to clicks under water.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
example_chart.note: These results are made up, to show what a finished table can look like. Write down what you really hear.

setup.art: A steel spoon tied by its handle to the middle of a metre of string, lying on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Tie the spoon to the middle of the string.

setup.art: A child leaning forward with one end of the string wound round each first finger, the spoon hanging free in front of her knees.
setup.caption: 2. Wind one end round each first finger. Let the spoon hang free.

setup.art: The same child with her fingertips pressed against the front of her ear holes, while a grown-up taps the hanging spoon with another spoon.
setup.caption: 3. Press your fingertips to your ears. A helper taps the spoon.

setup.art: A notebook table with rows for air, cotton string, wool and rubber bands.
setup.caption: 4. Count the seconds you hear the ring. Write them down.

flow.do: 1. Tie the handle of the spoon to the middle of the cotton string. 2. Your child winds one end twice round each first finger. 3. They lean forward so that the spoon hangs free. 4. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: First you will hear the spoon through the air. Then you will hear it through the string. Which way will the ring last longer? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Tie the spoon to the middle of the string. Wind the ends round your first fingers. Guess which way sounds longer. Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: Air is what sound normally travels through, so air will be best.
The string touches the spoon, so the vibration can run along it.
A string is too thin to carry a sound.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Spoon on a String. You hang a spoon on a string and guess how its ring will reach you best.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds the string with hands away from the ears. 2. Tap the spoon gently with the second spoon. 3. Your child counts the seconds until the ring fades. 4. Do it three times. 5. Now they press their fingertips against their ears, and you tap three more times.
flow.say: Hold your hands away from your ears and count how long you hear the ring. Now press your fingertips to your ears, and count again. What is different?
flow.kid: Hands away from ears first. Count the seconds of ringing. Then fingertips on your ears. Count again.

check.q: In the Spoon on a String, what is the vibration travelling through when your fingers are at your ears?
options: The string, your fingers and your head bones
Only the air in the room
Nothing at all
check.why: The vibration runs along the solid string and into your fingers. Then it passes through the bones of your head to the inner ear. If you chose the air, notice that the sound was much weaker when your hands were away from your ears.

flow.parent: Through the air the spoon gives a thin 'tink' for a second or two. Through the string it sounds like a large bell, and rings for much longer. Count seconds by saying 'one thousand and one, one thousand and two'.
flow.context: In this step of the Spoon on a String you hear the tapped spoon through the air. Then you hear it through the string, with your fingertips at your ears.

flow.do: 1. Untie the spoon and tie it to the wool. Tap three times and count. 2. Do the same with the chain of rubber bands. 3. Go back to the cotton string. While the spoon rings, pinch the string with two fingers halfway along.
flow.say: Now the wool, then the rubber bands. Count each time. Last, I will pinch the string while the spoon is ringing. What do you think you will hear?
flow.kid: Try wool. Then try rubber bands. Count each time. Then someone pinches the string. What happens?
flow.parent: Rubber bands usually carry the ring worst. Soft, stretchy rubber takes the energy out of the vibration. Wool often falls in between. Write down what you really hear. A pinch on the string cuts the ring off at once, because the fingers take the vibration.
flow.context: In this step of the Spoon on a String you swap the string for wool, then for rubber bands. Then someone pinches the string while the spoon rings.

flow.do: 1. Half fill the bucket with water. 2. Your child presses one ear against the outside of the bucket and covers the other ear. 3. Hold two spoons under the water and click them together.
flow.say: Sound has crossed air and string. Can it cross water? Press your ear to the bucket. Tell me if you hear the spoons click under the water.
flow.kid: Press one ear to the bucket. Cover the other ear. Can you hear the spoons click under water?
flow.parent: The clicks are heard clearly. The vibration crossed the water and the wall of the bucket to reach the ear. So sound travels through liquids too.
flow.context: In this step of the Spoon on a String two spoons are clicked together under water in a bucket. It shows whether a vibration crosses a liquid.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they heard, and why they think it happened. 3. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your counts. Say what you thought would happen, what you heard, and why you think it happened. Why was the ring so much stronger through the string?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you heard. Say why you think it happened.

ask.q: Why did the spoon sound so much louder through the string?
good: The vibration ran straight along the string and did not spread out.
A small spoon pushes very little air, but it can shake a string.

ask.q: Name the three kinds of medium the vibration crossed today.
good: A gas, which was the air.
A solid, which was the string.
A liquid, which was the water.

flow.parent: Everything is made of particles. A sound travels when each particle pushes the next. A spoon is small, so it pushes very little air. In the air the sound also spreads out in all directions. Along the string, the vibration is passed straight to your fingers and bones. So far more of it reaches the inner ear. The slow, deep vibrations of the spoon travel well along the string. That is why it sounds like a big bell.
flow.think: Doctors listen to a heart through a stethoscope. Which idea from this test does a stethoscope use?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Spoon on a String. You say what your counts show about sound in solids, liquids and gases.

activities.title: The Blur and the Pinch: what is a humming thing doing?
activities.context: This is a short activity to start the unit. You pluck a rubber band and ring a steel tumbler, look closely, and then stop each sound with a touch.

materials.item: a rubber band
a steel tumbler and a steel spoon
a strip of paper about as long and as wide as a finger

schedule.what: Pluck a rubber band on a tumbler, look at the blur, and stop the sound with a touch.

activities.record: Write two things you noticed and one thing you wonder.

setup.art: A rubber band stretched lengthwise over a steel tumbler, so that it crosses the open mouth.
setup.caption: 1. Stretch a rubber band over the open mouth of a tumbler.

setup.art: The band just after a pluck, drawn as a blur that is wide in the middle and thin at the rim.
setup.caption: 2. Pluck the band. Look at it from the side.

setup.art: A fingertip touching the blurred band, and beside it two fingers pinching the rim of a ringing tumbler.
setup.caption: 3. Touch the band. Then ring the tumbler and pinch its rim.

flow.do: 1. Stretch the rubber band lengthwise over the tumbler, so that it crosses the open mouth. 2. Your child plucks the band over the mouth. 3. They look at it from the side, at eye level.
flow.say: Pluck the band and look at it from the side. What do you notice? Where is the blur widest? What do you wonder?
flow.kid: Pluck the band. Look from the side. Where is the blur widest? What do you wonder?

ask.q: What do you notice?
good: The band looks like a blur.
The blur is widest in the middle and thin at the rim.
The hum gets softer as the blur gets thinner.

flow.parent: Do not explain yet. Write down what your child notices and wonders. The unit comes back to these questions.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Blur and the Pinch. You pluck a rubber band stretched over a tumbler and look at it closely.

flow.do: 1. Your child plucks the band again and touches it lightly with one fingertip. 2. Then they pluck it and hold the edge of the paper strip so that it just touches the band.
flow.say: Pluck it and touch it lightly. What does your finger feel? What happens to the hum? Now let the paper just touch the band. What do you hear?
flow.kid: Pluck the band and touch it lightly. What do you feel? Now touch it with the paper strip.
flow.parent: The finger feels a tickle, and the hum stops at once. The paper buzzes, because the band hits it again and again, very quickly.
flow.context: In this step of the Blur and the Pinch you touch the humming rubber band with a finger. Then you touch it with a strip of paper.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds the tumbler by its base and taps the rim with the spoon. 2. While it rings, they pinch the rim with two fingers. 3. Ask the two questions and write down the answers.
flow.say: Ring the tumbler, then pinch the rim. What happened to the sound? What was the band doing while it hummed? Why did it carry on after your finger let go?
flow.kid: Ring the tumbler. Pinch the rim. What happened to the sound? What was the band doing?

check.q: A ringing tumbler goes silent when you pinch its rim. What does that show?
options: The sound lasts only while the tumbler vibrates
Fingers soak up sound from the air
The tumbler ran out of sound
check.why: The pinch stops the tumbler moving, and the sound stops at the same moment. So the sound comes from the vibration. A thing does not hold a store of sound that can run out.

flow.parent: Keep your child's answer to the last question. The Slow String activity answers it.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Blur and the Pinch. You ring a steel tumbler and stop the sound by pinching the rim.

activities.title: The Slow String: watch one vibration
activities.context: In this activity you make a string from a chain of rubber bands. It vibrates slowly enough to watch. Then you make it faster, until it is a blur and gives a note.

materials.item: rubber bands, looped together into a chain about 40 cm long
a chair, a window grille or a door handle to tie one end to
a clothes peg

schedule.what: Make a slow string from a chain of rubber bands and watch one vibration. Then tighten and shorten it until it gives a note.

activities.record: Draw the chain at three moments of one swing: far to one side, passing the middle, and far to the other side. Mark where it was fastest and where it stopped.

setup.art: Six rubber bands looped one through the next to make a chain, one end tied to the back of a chair, the other held in a child's hand.
setup.caption: 1. Loop six rubber bands into a chain. Tie one end to a chair.

setup.art: The chain held almost slack with a clothes peg clipped to its middle, drawn in three positions as it swings from side to side.
setup.caption: 2. Clip a peg to the middle. Pull it aside and let go. Watch the swing.

setup.art: The child standing two steps further back with the chain pulled tight and drawn as a blur.
setup.caption: 3. Take the peg off. Step back to tighten the chain. Pluck again.

setup.art: Two fingers pinching the tight chain a hand-width from the end, and the short part being plucked.
setup.caption: 4. Pinch the chain to make a short part. Pluck the short part and listen.

flow.do: 1. Loop six rubber bands into a chain. 2. Tie one end to a chair. 3. Hold the other end so that the chain is just straight and hardly stretched. 4. Clip the peg to the middle. 5. Pull the peg a hand-width to one side and let go.
flow.say: This chain is a string, but a slow one. Pull the peg to the side and let go. Watch one full trip. Where does the peg stop for a moment? Where is it moving fastest?
flow.kid: Clip the peg to the middle of the chain. Pull it to the side. Let go and watch. Where is it fastest?

ask.q: Where is the peg moving fastest, and where does it stop for a moment?
good: It is fastest in the middle, at the rest position.
It stops for a moment at each side, then turns back.

flow.parent: With the peg on, the chain swings about 3 times a second. If it is too quick to follow, hold the chain a little looser or add a second peg.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Slow String. You watch a chain of rubber bands with a peg on it swing slowly from side to side.

flow.do: 1. Ask the question below before you explain anything. 2. Let your child watch several swings. 3. Then read them the explanation in the note.
flow.say: The chain pulls the peg back towards the middle. So why does the peg not stop when it gets to the middle? Watch again, and tell me what you think.
flow.kid: The chain pulls the peg to the middle. Why does the peg not stop there? Watch again.

ask.q: Why does the peg not stop in the middle?
good: It is moving fastest there, so it carries on.
Nothing stops it in the middle. The pull only starts again once it has gone past.

flow.parent: The stretched chain pulls the peg back towards its rest position. The peg speeds up all the way there, so it arrives at full speed and goes past. On the other side the chain pulls it back again. Each swing is a little smaller, because some energy leaves each time.
flow.context: In this step of the Slow String you watch the peg on the chain go past the middle. You work out why it does not stop there.

flow.do: 1. Take the peg off and pluck the chain. 2. Your child takes one step back to tighten the chain, and plucks. 3. They take one more step back, and pluck again.
flow.say: Now take the peg off. Is the swing faster or slower? Why? Now step back to pull the chain tighter. What happens to the swing?
flow.kid: Take the peg off. Pluck. Is it faster? Step back and pluck again. What changes?

check.q: Taking the peg off the Slow String made it swing faster. Why?
options: There was less weight to move
The chain became longer
The peg was holding the sound in
check.why: The chain pulls back just as hard, but with the peg gone it has less weight to move. So each trip takes less time. The length of the chain did not change.

flow.parent: Without the peg, the chain flutters too fast to count. Pulled tight, it becomes a blur, widest in the middle, and you may hear a faint low hum. A tighter chain pulls back harder, so it vibrates faster.
flow.context: In this step of the Slow String you take the peg off the chain of rubber bands. Then you pull the chain tighter.

flow.do: 1. Keep the chain tight. 2. Pinch it with two fingers about 10 cm from your child's hand. 3. Your child plucks the short part and listens. 4. Ask what they thought would happen, what happened and why.
flow.say: Now I will pinch the chain, so that only a short part can move. Pluck the short part. What do you hear? Say what you thought would happen, what happened, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Pluck the short part of the chain. What do you hear? Say why you think it happened.

ask.q: The same chain gave a slow swing, then a blur, then a note. What changed each time?
good: First the weight, when the peg came off.
Then the tightness, when I stepped back.
Then the length, when it was pinched short.

flow.parent: The short part gives a clear twang. A short string has less to move, so it vibrates faster. A slow vibration that you can watch and a fast vibration that you can hear are the same kind of movement. Only the frequency is different.
flow.think: A veena player presses a string against a fret to play a higher note. Which of your three changes is that?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Slow String. You pluck a short part of the tight chain of rubber bands and hear a clear note.

activities.title: The Palm Pipe: play an air column with a slap
activities.context: In this activity you slap the end of a cardboard tube with your palm and hear a note. The note comes from the air inside the tube. You compare a long tube with a short one.

materials.item: cardboard tubes from kitchen foil or cling film, about 30 cm long. Or roll an old notebook cover into a tube 3 to 4 cm wide and tape it
scissors or a knife, for a grown-up to cut one tube in half
an empty plastic bottle with its cap

schedule.what: Slap the end of a long tube and of a short tube with your palm. Compare the notes of the two air columns.

activities.record: Draw the long tube and the short tube. Under each one write 'higher note' or 'lower note'.

setup.art: A child squeezing an empty plastic bottle with the cap on, the sides pushing back against her fingers.
setup.caption: 1. Squeeze a closed empty bottle. Feel the air push back.

setup.art: A child holding a cardboard tube upright in one hand and slapping its top end with the flat palm of the other hand.
setup.caption: 2. Slap one end of the long tube with your palm, and keep your palm there.

setup.art: A long tube and a tube half as long, side by side, with a low musical note drawn above the long one and a high note above the short one.
setup.caption: 3. Do the same with the short tube. Which note is higher?

flow.do: 1. Screw the cap on the empty bottle. 2. Your child squeezes it and lets go. 3. Take the cap off and squeeze again.
flow.say: Squeeze the closed bottle. What do you feel? Now take the cap off and squeeze again. What is different?
flow.kid: Squeeze the closed bottle. Does it push back? Now take the cap off and squeeze.
flow.parent: With the cap on, the trapped air pushes back like a spring. With the cap off, the air just flows out. Springy air is what lets an air column vibrate.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Palm Pipe. You squeeze a closed bottle to feel that air is springy.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds the long tube upright in one hand. 2. They slap the top end with the flat of the other palm, and keep the palm on the end. 3. Ask for a guess: will a tube half as long sound higher, lower or the same? Ask why.
flow.say: Slap the end and keep your palm there. Listen for the note inside the 'pop'. Now guess. I will cut the other tube in half. Will the short tube sound higher, lower or the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Slap the end of the tube and keep your palm there. Hear the note. Will a short tube sound higher or lower? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: A short string was higher, so a short tube may be higher too.
There is less air to move in a short tube.

flow.parent: The slap squeezes the air in the tube. The air springs back and vibrates back and forth along the tube for a moment. That gives the 'pop' its note. A rolled paper tube gives a softer sound than a cardboard one.
flow.context: In this step of the Palm Pipe you slap the end of a long cardboard tube. Then you guess what a shorter tube will do.

flow.do: 1. Cut the second tube in half. 2. Your child slaps the long tube, then the short one, several times. 3. Ask what they thought would happen, what happened and why. 4. Then they hold the long tube to one ear and listen. They try it with the far end open, and then closed by a palm.
flow.say: Slap the long one, then the short one. Which is higher? Say what you thought would happen, what happened, and why you think it happened. Now hold the long tube to your ear and listen.
flow.kid: Slap the long tube. Slap the short tube. Which is higher? Say why you think it happened.

check.q: A 30 cm tube and a 15 cm tube are each slapped on one end. Which gives the higher note?
options: The 15 cm tube
The 30 cm tube
Both give the same note
check.why: A shorter air column has less air to move, so it vibrates faster and gives a higher note. If you chose the long tube, think of the Slow String: the short part gave the higher note too.

flow.parent: The short tube gives the higher note. With the tube at your ear you hear a faint steady hum, picked out of the noise of the room. It drops lower when a palm closes the far end. This last part is faint, so try it in a room with a fan running.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Palm Pipe. You compare the notes of a long tube and a short tube when each is slapped with a palm.

activities.title: Sss and Zzz: find the vibration in your throat
activities.context: In this activity you rest your fingers on your throat and say pairs of sounds. You find out which sounds use the vocal folds, and what the folds need in order to vibrate.

materials.item: your own voice and fingers

schedule.what: Feel your throat while you say 'sss' and 'zzz', then hum and pinch your nose.

activities.record: Make two lists: sounds with a buzz in the throat, and sounds without.

setup.art: A child resting two fingertips lightly on the bump at the front of her throat while saying 'zzz'.
setup.caption: 1. Rest two fingers on the front of your throat. Say 'sss', then 'zzz'.

setup.art: The same child humming with her lips closed and pinching her nose shut with her other hand.
setup.caption: 2. Hum with your lips closed. Then pinch your nose.

flow.do: 1. Your child rests two fingertips lightly on the bump at the front of the throat. 2. They say a long 'sss', then a long 'zzz'. 3. They do the same with 'fff' and 'vvv'.
flow.say: Rest your fingers on your throat. Say a long 'sss'. Now a long 'zzz'. What do your fingers feel? Try 'fff' and 'vvv'.
flow.kid: Fingers on your throat. Say 'sss'. Say 'zzz'. Which one buzzes? Try 'fff' and 'vvv'.
flow.parent: 'Zzz' and 'vvv' buzz under the fingers. 'Sss' and 'fff' do not. The mouth is in the same shape for each pair. The only difference is whether the vocal folds vibrate.
flow.context: This is the first step of Sss and Zzz. You feel your throat while you say pairs of sounds.

flow.do: 1. Ask for a guess first: what will happen to a hum if the nose is pinched shut? 2. Your child hums with lips closed. 3. While humming, they pinch the nose shut.
flow.say: Hum with your lips closed. What will happen if you pinch your nose while you hum? Why do you think so? Now try it.
flow.kid: Hum with your lips closed. Guess what a pinched nose will do. Now pinch your nose.

ask.q: The hum stopped. Why?
good: The air could not get out, so it stopped flowing.
The vocal folds need moving breath to keep vibrating.

flow.parent: The hum stops within a second. With the lips and the nose both shut, the breath cannot flow. The vocal folds vibrate only while air passes between them.
flow.context: In this step of Sss and Zzz you hum with your lips closed and then pinch your nose shut.

flow.do: 1. Your child keeps the fingers on the throat and slides a hum from low to high. 2. Ask what the bump in the throat does. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Slide your hum from as low as you can to as high as you can. What does the bump under your fingers do? What do you think is changing inside?
flow.kid: Hum from low to high. What does the bump in your throat do?

check.q: What do your vocal folds do to make a higher note?
options: They stretch tighter and vibrate faster
They stop moving
They push out more air
check.why: Tighter folds are pulled back harder, so they vibrate faster, as a tighter string does. More air makes a voice louder, but it does not make the note higher.

flow.parent: The voice box rises a little for high notes. Muscles stretch the folds longer, thinner and tighter, so they open and close more times each second.
flow.context: This is the last step of Sss and Zzz. You slide a hum from low to high and feel your voice box move.

projects.title: The Dancing Light Spot: a skin that shows your voice
projects.context: In this two-day project you build a small skin with a tiny mirror on it. Light bounces off the mirror onto a wall. When you speak at the skin, the spot of light moves, and you measure how far.

materials.item: a paper cup, or a piece of cardboard tube about 10 cm long
a balloon
a rubber band
a small flat mirror about 1 cm across, such as an embroidery mirror, a mirror sequin or a mirror bindi
glue or double-sided tape
a torch or a phone torch, or a beam of sunlight from a window
a ruler, sticky tape, a few books and a pale wall in a dim room

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the cup and the balloon. Do not use a laser pointer: it can harm eyes. Never shine the torch or the sunlight into anyone's eyes.

schedule.what: Build the skin with its mirror, let the glue dry, and find the spot of light on the wall.
Speak softly and loudly, low and high, at the skin. Measure how long the streak of light becomes each time.

projects.record: Draw the shape the spot makes for a soft 'aaa', a loud 'aaa', a low hum and a high hum. Beside each drawing write the length of the streak in centimetres.

setup.art: A paper cup with its bottom cut out and a piece of balloon stretched over the wide end, held by a rubber band, with a tiny mirror glued a little off the centre.
setup.caption: 1. Stretch a balloon skin over the cup. Glue a tiny mirror on it, a little off the centre.

setup.art: The cup taped on a stack of books, a phone torch shining on the mirror, and a bright spot of light on the wall.
setup.caption: 2. Shine a torch on the mirror. Find the spot of light on the wall.

setup.art: A child singing into the open end of the cup while the spot on the wall stretches into a line, and a ruler held beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Sing into the cup. Measure the streak the spot makes.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts the bottom out of the cup, and cuts the neck off the balloon. 2. Stretch the balloon over the wide end of the cup and hold it with the rubber band. 3. Glue the mirror to the skin, about halfway between the centre and the edge. 4. Leave the glue to dry.
flow.say: This balloon is our skin. The mirror will ride on it. If the skin moves, the mirror tilts. Why might a mirror be a good way to see a very small movement?
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts the cup and the balloon. Stretch the balloon over the cup. Glue the mirror on, a little off the centre.
flow.parent: The skin should be tight and flat. The mirror goes off the centre because the skin tilts most there. At the exact centre the mirror only moves in and out, and the spot hardly shifts.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Dancing Light Spot. You build a balloon skin on a cup and glue a tiny mirror to it.

flow.do: 1. Tape the cup on its side on a stack of books. The skin should face a pale wall 1 to 2 metres away. 2. Make the room dim. 3. Shine the torch on the mirror from the side. 4. Move the torch until a spot of light lands on the wall. 5. Mark the middle of the spot with a pencil dot.
flow.say: Let us find the spot. The light goes from the torch to the mirror and then to the wall. Now clap near the cup. Does the spot move?
flow.kid: Shine the torch on the mirror. Find the spot on the wall. Clap near the cup. Does the spot move?
flow.parent: The spot from a torch is a fuzzy patch a few centimetres wide. That is fine. Sunlight from a window gives a sharper spot. The further away the wall is, the more the spot moves.
flow.context: In this step of the Dancing Light Spot you shine a torch on the tiny mirror. You find its spot of light on the wall.

flow.do: 1. Ask for a guess first: will a loud 'aaa' move the spot more than a soft one? Why? 2. Your child speaks into the open end of the cup: a soft 'aaa', then a loud 'aaa'. 3. A helper holds the ruler at the wall and measures the streak each time. 4. Then try a low hum and a high hum, equally loud.
flow.say: Guess first. Will a loud 'aaa' change the spot more than a soft 'aaa'? Why do you think so? Now sing into the cup, and I will measure the streak.
flow.kid: Guess first. Then sing a soft 'aaa' into the cup. Then a loud one. Measure the streak each time.

ask.q: What did the loud 'aaa' do to the spot, compared with the soft one?
good: The streak was longer.
The skin moved further, so the mirror tilted more.

flow.parent: A louder sound gives a longer streak, because the skin has a bigger amplitude. Low and high notes often give different shapes. Some notes move the skin much more than others. If the spot does not move, bring the mouth closer, and check that the skin is tight.
flow.context: In this step of the Dancing Light Spot you sing into the cup, softly and then loudly. You measure how far the spot of light moves.

flow.do: 1. Look at the drawings and the lengths together. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. 3. Ask what in their own body works like this skin.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Your voice never touched the skin. What carried the vibration there?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why you think it happened.

check.q: A louder voice made a longer streak of light. What does that show about the skin?
options: It vibrated with a bigger amplitude
It vibrated more times each second
It stopped vibrating
check.why: A louder sound pushes the skin further from its rest position each time. That is a bigger amplitude. The number of vibrations each second depends on the note, not on the loudness.

flow.parent: The voice pushes the air, the air pushes the skin, and the mirror shows the movement. A microphone works in the same way: a thin skin moves with the sound, and the movement is turned into an electric signal.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Dancing Light Spot. You say what the moving spot of light shows about a skin and a voice.

challenges.title: Quiet the Buzz: a stand for a buzzing phone
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. A phone on vibrate is loud on a steel plate, because the plate vibrates too. You design a stand that keeps the vibration out of the plate.
challenges.problem: A phone set to vibrate lies on an upturned steel plate. When it buzzes, the rattle can be heard across the flat. Build a stand for the phone that sits on the same plate. The buzz must be as quiet as you can make it. The phone must lie on top where you can see the whole screen.
constraints: The stand must sit on the steel plate. You may not move the plate.
The phone must lie on top of the stand, with its whole screen showing. You may not wrap it or cover it.
The phone must stay on the stand while it buzzes for 10 seconds.
Use only things from home, such as cloth, sponge, erasers, rubber bands, bottle caps, card and rice.
materials: a phone set to vibrate, and a second phone to call it, or a timer set to vibrate
a kitchen sponge, a folded towel, erasers and rubber bands
bottle caps, card and a small box
a handful of rice in a shallow lid
general: Put a thick, soft pad under the phone, such as a sponge or a folded towel.
Stand the phone on four soft feet, such as four erasers.
Hang the phone in a sling of rubber bands stretched across a small box.
creative: Rest the phone on a bed of rice in a shallow lid. The grains rub against each other and take the energy.
Put a heavy book between the phone and a soft pad. A heavy thing is harder to shake.
Stack two different soft layers, such as sponge on cloth, and test whether two layers beat one.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own stand. Draw it, build it and test it with the walk-away test. From how many steps away can you still hear the buzz? Write which idea worked best, and why you think it did.

setup.art: A phone lying on an upturned steel plate on a table, with zigzag lines around both to show a loud rattle.
setup.caption: 1. Hear how loud the phone is when it buzzes on the bare plate.

setup.art: The same phone resting on four erasers on the plate, with the screen showing.
setup.caption: 2. Build a stand that keeps the vibration out of the plate.

setup.art: A child walking backwards away from the table, counting steps, with one hand cupped behind her ear.
setup.caption: 3. Walk away until you cannot hear the buzz. Count the steps.

flow.do: 1. Set the phone to vibrate and lay it on the upturned steel plate. 2. Call it from another phone. 3. Your child walks away, one step at a time, until the buzz cannot be heard. 4. Write down the number of steps. 5. Then do the same with the phone held in a hand.
flow.say: First let us hear the problem. How many steps away can you still hear the buzz? Now I will hold the phone in my hand. Is it louder or quieter? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Lay the phone on the plate and make it buzz. Walk away until it is silent. Count your steps.

ask.q: The phone is the same. Why is it so much louder on the plate than in a hand?
good: The plate vibrates too, and it is big, so it pushes more air.
The hand is soft and takes the vibration.

flow.parent: A phone buzzes because a tiny motor inside spins a weight that is off its centre. The phone is small, so it pushes little air. On the plate, the whole plate is made to vibrate and acts as a soundboard.
flow.context: This is the first step of Quiet the Buzz. You measure how far away a buzzing phone can be heard when it lies on a bare steel plate.

flow.do: 1. Read the usual ideas together: a soft pad, soft feet and a sling. 2. Your child chooses one, builds it and tests it with the walk-away test. 3. They change one thing and test again.
flow.say: Which idea do you want to try first? Why do you think it will work? Test it the same way each time, so that the test is fair.
flow.kid: Pick one idea. Build it. Make the phone buzz. Count your steps again.
flow.parent: Keep the room equally quiet for every test, and start walking from the same spot. Switch off a noisy fan if you can.
flow.context: In this step of Quiet the Buzz you build a stand for the buzzing phone. Then you test how far away the buzz can still be heard.

flow.do: 1. Compare the step counts. 2. Ask which stand was best and why. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Which stand gave the fewest steps? What did it do to the vibration? Where do you see pads like this in our home?
flow.kid: Which stand was quietest? What did it do to the vibration?

check.q: Why is a buzzing phone quieter on a sponge than on a steel plate?
options: The sponge keeps the vibration from the plate
The sponge makes the phone's motor spin slower
Sound cannot travel through air near a sponge
check.why: The phone's motor spins just the same. The soft sponge takes the energy of the vibration. So the wide plate is not made to vibrate and push the air.

flow.parent: Look for the same idea at home: rubber feet under a mixer-grinder, a mat under a washing machine, and rubber pads where a ceiling fan hangs.
flow.context: This is the last step of Quiet the Buzz. You compare your stands for the buzzing phone and say why the best one worked.

worksheets.title: What vibrates, and how the sound reaches you (core)

items.p: What is a vibration?
opts: A movement back and forth, again and again
A movement in one direction only
items.why: A vibrating thing moves to one side of its rest position and back through it to the other side. It does this over and over. Choosing 'a loud sound' mixes up the sound with the movement that makes it.

items.p: True or false: a thing can make a sound without any part of it vibrating.
items.why: False. Every sound source vibrates. In the Blur and the Pinch, the tumbler went silent the moment its vibration was stopped.

items.p: The number of vibrations in one second is called the ____.
items.why: Frequency is counted in hertz. One hertz is one vibration each second.

items.p: Match each sound maker to the part that vibrates.
items.why: Strings, skins and air columns are the three main vibrating things in instruments. A voice starts with the vocal folds in the voice box.

items.p: In the Comb Test, why did a quick stroke give a note and not ticks?
opts: The ticks came too fast to hear apart
items.why: The comb, the card and the teeth were the same. Only the number of ticks each second changed. Above about 20 a second, the ear hears them as one note.

items.p: Sort these instruments by what vibrates: a string, a skin or an air column.
items.why: A sitar and a violin have strings. A tabla and a chenda have skins. In a nadaswaram and a conch, the air inside vibrates.

items.p: A veena is plucked. Put these in the order the vibration passes through them.
items.why: The string makes the body vibrate, the body pushes the air, and the air makes the eardrum vibrate. The ear bones pass the vibration to the inner ear.

items.p: True or false: sound can travel through a solid, a liquid and a gas.
items.why: True. In the Spoon on a String, the ring crossed air, ran along a string and passed through water. Each one is made of particles that pass the push on.

items.p: A card crosses 40 teeth of a comb in 2 seconds. How many ticks is that each second?
items.why: 40 ticks shared over 2 seconds is 40 ÷ 2, which is 20 ticks each second.

items.p: In the Thali and the Skin, what did you change on purpose?
opts: The distance from the plate to the bowl
items.why: The distance was the independent variable, the one thing changed on purpose. The grains, the bowl and the spoon were control variables, kept the same.

items.p: You pinch the rim of a ringing steel tumbler, and the sound stops. Explain why, in two sentences.
items.a: The sound comes from the tumbler vibrating. The pinch stops the vibration, so the tumbler no longer pushes the air, and the sound stops.
items.why: A strong answer says that the sound lasts only as long as the vibration. It also says that fingers take the energy of the vibration.

items.p: In the Spoon on a String, the spoon sounded far louder with your fingers at your ears. Explain why.
items.a: With my fingers at my ears, the vibration ran along the solid string. It passed into my fingers and the bones of my head. It did not spread out in all directions, as it does in air. So much more of it reached my inner ear.
items.why: A strong answer names the path, which is string, fingers and bone. It also says that sound in the air spreads out, so less of it arrives.

items.p: Draw a plucked string as it looks while it hums. Mark its rest position, and mark where it moves most.
items.a: A blur shaped like a thin lens between two fixed ends. A straight line through the middle of the blur is the rest position. The widest part of the blur, halfway along, is where the string moves most.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the ends still and the middle moving most. The rest position is a straight line between the ends.
items.art: Two fixed pegs with a blank space between them for the child's drawing.

items.p: Which matters more for the sound of a veena: the string or the hollow body?

views.says: The string. Without the string nothing vibrates, and the string sets the note.
The body. A string by itself pushes so little air that you can hardly hear it.
Neither works alone. The string decides the note, and the body decides how much air is pushed.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you found in this unit. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that the note changes when the string is tightened or shortened. Another is that a buzzing phone was much louder on a steel plate, which acted as a soundboard.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer uses evidence. The Slow String shows what sets the note. Quiet the Buzz shows what a wide surface does.

items.p: Why can sound not cross empty space?
opts: No particles are there to pass the push
items.why: A sound travels when each particle pushes the next. Empty space has no particles, so the vibration has nothing to travel through.

worksheets.title: Why a vibration is fast or slow (stretch)

items.p: Where is a vibrating string moving fastest?
opts: As it passes its rest position
At the far edge of its swing
It moves at one speed everywhere
items.why: The string speeds up all the way back to its rest position and slows down after it. At the far edge it stops for an instant. The fixed ends do not move at all.

items.p: In the Slow String, a clothes peg on the chain made it swing more slowly. Why?
opts: There was more weight to move
The chain was pulled back harder
items.why: The chain pulled back just as hard as before. It had more weight to move, so each trip took longer.

items.p: True or false: plucking a string harder makes it vibrate more times each second.
items.why: False. A harder pluck gives a bigger amplitude and a louder sound. The frequency, and so the note, stays the same.

items.p: The lowest string of a guitar has fine wire wound round it. What is the wire for?
opts: To add weight, so it vibrates slowly
items.why: More weight to move gives a slower vibration and a lower note. The string can then stay tight enough to ring well.

items.p: Three of these make a string vibrate faster. Which one makes it slower?
opts: Pressing it to make it shorter
Changing it for a lighter string
items.why: Winding wire round a string adds weight, so it vibrates more slowly. A tighter, shorter or lighter string vibrates faster.

items.p: A honeybee's wings beat about 230 times a second. How many times do they beat in 2 seconds?
items.why: About 230 beats each second for 2 seconds is 230 × 2, which is about 460 beats.

items.p: Does each change make the vibration faster or slower?
items: pressing wet paste onto a drum skin
covering more holes on a flute
items.why: A harder pull back, or less to move, gives a faster vibration. More weight, or a longer air column, gives a slower one.

items.p: The distance a vibrating thing moves from its rest position is called its ____.
items.why: Amplitude is the size of a vibration. A bigger amplitude gives a louder sound.

items.p: A card crosses 40 comb teeth. Put the strokes in order, from the lowest sound to the highest.
items: A stroke of half a second
a: A stroke of half a second
items.why: The strokes give 10, 20, 40 and 80 ticks each second. More ticks each second give a higher sound.

items.p: In the Palm Pipe, the short tube gave a higher note than the long tube. Explain why.
items.a: The note came from the air inside the tube vibrating back and forth. The short tube holds less air, so there is less to move. The air column vibrates faster and gives a higher note.
items.why: A strong answer says that the air column vibrates. It links a shorter column to less air to move and a faster vibration.

items.p: A phone buzzes on a steel plate, then on a folded towel. Predict which is louder, and explain.
items.a: The phone is louder on the steel plate. The plate is hard, so the phone makes the whole plate vibrate. The wide plate pushes a lot of air. The soft towel takes the energy of the vibration, so only the small phone pushes the air.
items.why: A strong answer says that the plate acts as a soundboard and that the towel damps the vibration. It may use the step counts from Quiet the Buzz.

items.p: Plan a fair test: do rava or rice grains jump more on a skin? Name your three kinds of variable.
items.a: I change the kind of grain: that is the independent variable. I measure how much the grains move, with a score of 2, 1 or 0: that is the dependent variable. I keep the same bowl, film, plate, spoon, strike and distance: those are the control variables. I do three strikes for each grain.
items.why: A strong plan changes one thing only, and says what is measured and how. It lists what stays the same, and repeats each test.

items.p: Are vibrations slower than 20 a second, which humans cannot hear, still sound?

views.says: No. Sound is what we hear. If no person can hear it, it is only a shaking of the air.
Yes. Elephants hear these slow rumbles and answer them from far away. For an elephant they are sound.
The air does the same thing at 15 vibrations a second as at 50. 'Sound' is our word for the part our ears catch.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then say what one of the other views gets right.
items.a: Any view with a reason. One reason is that the Comb Test shows the air carrying pushes whether or not they blend into a note. Another is that different animals hear different ranges, so one animal's silence is another's sound.
items.why: This is a real disagreement about what the word 'sound' should mean. A strong answer uses a fact from the unit and treats another view fairly.

items.p: Label this picture of a sound reaching an ear: source, medium, eardrum, ear bones, inner ear.
a: Medium: the air between the drum and the ear
Eardrum: the small tight skin at the end of the ear hole
Ear bones: the three tiny bones behind the eardrum
Inner ear: the coiled part filled with liquid
items.why: The vibration starts at the source, crosses the medium, and makes the eardrum vibrate. The bones pass it to the liquid of the inner ear.
items.art: A drum on the left, dotted air in the middle, and a cut-away ear on the right, with five blank label lines.

items.p: True or false: a plucked string moves most at its two ends.
items.why: False. The ends are held still. The string moves most in the middle, where the blur is widest.

items.p: A bell rings inside a jar while the air is pumped out. What happens?
opts: The bell still moves, but its sound fades
items.why: The bell still vibrates, but with fewer and fewer air particles there is less to carry the pushes. Robert Boyle and Robert Hooke showed this about 1660.

items.p: The quartz crystal in a watch vibrates 32,768 times a second. What best explains such a high frequency?
opts: It is very stiff and very small
It is very soft and very heavy
items.why: A stiff thing is pulled back hard, and a tiny thing has little to move. Both make a vibration fast. Hitting harder changes only the amplitude.

items.p: True or false: after a very large earthquake, the whole Earth can ring for weeks.
items.why: True. The Earth is springy and has weight, so it vibrates when struck. After the Sumatra earthquake of 2004 it rang for weeks, far too slowly to hear.

items.p: True or false: the air next to a drum travels across the room to your ear.
items.why: False. Each air particle moves a tiny way and comes back. It pushes the next particle, and the push travels across the room.

items.p: Match each wrong idea to the evidence against it.
pairs: Sound is tiny particles thrown from the source
A bell in an airless jar goes quiet
The voice is a flute, and no solid part vibrates
Holding the vocal folds still stops the sound
A note is a different kind of sound from a tick
Fast ticks on a comb become a note
A harder pluck gives a higher note
The note stays the same when you pluck harder
items.why: Each wrong idea was reasonable until someone tested it. The test in each pair is one that the idea cannot explain.

items.p: A card crosses 80 teeth in half a second. How many ticks is that each second?
items.why: 80 ticks in half a second means twice as many in a whole second. 80 × 2 is 160 ticks each second.

items.p: A wide surface that a string makes vibrate, so that more air is pushed, is called a ____.
items.why: A thin string pushes very little air. The soundboard is wide, so it pushes much more, and the instrument is louder.

items.p: In the Spoon on a String, the spoon sounded deeper through the string than through the air. Why?
opts: Its slow vibrations hardly push the air
The string slowed the spoon down
The air removed the high notes
items.why: A spoon vibrates in fast ways and slow ways at once. A small spoon pushes the air poorly with its slow vibrations, but they travel well along the string. So the deep part of the ring is heard only through the string.

items.p: Someone says, 'Heavy things always make low notes.' Give one example that fits and one that does not.
items.a: It fits a big bell, which rings lower than a small bell of the same metal. It does not fit a heavy string that is pulled very tight. That string can sound higher than a light, slack one. The note depends on two things together: the weight to move and how hard it is pulled back.
items.why: A strong answer shows that weight is only one of the two things that set the frequency. The other is the strength of the pull back.

items.p: One strike of a plate 80 cm away made the grains jump. Give two possible reasons, and a check.
items.a: Someone may have bumped the table, or that strike may have been much harder than the others. To check, strike again several times at 80 cm with nobody touching the table. If the grains stay still, the one jump was an accident.
items.why: A strong answer treats one odd result as something to test again. It names causes other than the sound, and says how to rule them out.

items.p: Antoine Ferrein blew air through a voice box and tightened the bands inside it. The note rose. What did that show?
items.a: It showed that the bands must vibrate for there to be a voice. So the voice does not come only from air in the windpipe, as in a flute. It did not show how the bands move in a living person, which nobody had yet seen.
items.why: A strong answer says what the test proves, that the bands are the source. It also says what the test leaves open.

items.p: Two astronauts on the Moon touch helmets, and then they can hear each other speak. Explain how.
items.a: The Moon has no air, so there are no particles between the astronauts to carry a sound. When the helmets touch, a voice makes the air in one helmet vibrate. That makes the helmet vibrate, and the vibration passes through the solid helmets into the air of the other.
items.why: A strong answer says that sound needs a medium, and traces the path: air, solid helmet, solid helmet, air.

items.p: Do plants hear?

views.says: Yes. Thale cress plants made more defence chemicals after they felt the vibrations of a caterpillar chewing. They sensed a vibration and acted on it.
Responding to a shake is not hearing. A plant has no ear, and these studies should be repeated by other teams first.
It depends on the word. If hearing means sensing vibrations and acting on them, then plants hear.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Say what evidence would change your mind. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. A strong answer notes that a sound is a vibration and that a leaf can be shaken by it. It also says what would count as evidence, such as other teams finding the same result.
items.why: Plants sense vibrations and respond to them. Whether to call that hearing is argued. A strong answer keeps the finding and the word apart.

items.p: Draw air particles carrying one push from a drum skin to an ear. Show where the particles are crowded.
items.a: A row of dots from the drum to the ear. In one band the dots are crowded together, and on each side of it they are spread out as usual. An arrow shows the crowded band moving towards the ear. Small two-way arrows on single dots show that each particle only moves a little and comes back.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the crowded band travelling while the particles themselves stay in their own places.
items.art: A drum on the left and an ear on the right, with a blank space between them for the child's dots.

items.p: Put these vibrations in order, from the slowest to the fastest.
items: The whole Earth ringing: one vibration in 54 minutes
A cat's purr: about 25 each second
A honeybee's wings: about 230 each second
A quartz watch crystal: 32,768 each second
a: The whole Earth ringing: one vibration in 54 minutes
A cat's purr: about 25 each second
A honeybee's wings: about 230 each second
A quartz watch crystal: 32,768 each second
items.why: Big, heavy things vibrate slowly, and small, stiff things vibrate fast. The Earth is the biggest and the crystal is the smallest and stiffest.

quiz.p: Which words describe one full vibration of a string?
opts: To one side, across to the other, and back
From one end of the string to the other
quiz.why: One vibration is a full trip: away from the rest position, back through it, out to the other side and back again.

quiz.p: A string vibrates 440 times each second. What is its frequency?
quiz.why: Frequency is the number of vibrations each second, and its unit is the hertz. Metres measure length and seconds measure time.

quiz.p: Why does a plucked string go past its rest position, and not stop there?
opts: The finger is still pulling it
quiz.why: The string is pulled back towards its rest position and speeds up all the way. It arrives at full speed, so it carries on to the other side.

quiz.p: Which change makes a string vibrate faster?
quiz.why: A tighter string is pulled back harder, so it vibrates faster. Wire and extra length add more to move, which slows it. A harder pluck changes only the loudness.

quiz.p: A card gives 5 ticks a second on a comb, then 80. What do you hear?
opts: Separate ticks, then a low note
quiz.why: At 5 a second each tick is heard one by one. At 80 a second they come too fast to hear apart, so the ear hears a note.

quiz.p: A male cricket draws one wing across a row of teeth on the other. Which test is this like?
opts: The card drawn along a comb
The spoon hung on a string
The bottle squeezed with its cap on
quiz.why: Each tooth gives one push, as each comb tooth did. The teeth pass so quickly that the pushes blend into a note, which is the cricket's song.

quiz.p: What vibrates first when someone plays a nadaswaram?
opts: A cane reed, then the air column
quiz.why: The player's breath makes the cane reed flap, and the reed sets the air inside the long pipe vibrating. A nadaswaram has no skin and no string.

quiz.p: True or false: your vocal folds can go on vibrating when no breath is flowing.
quiz.why: False. Breath blows the folds apart and they spring shut, again and again. In Sss and Zzz, a hum stopped when the nose and the lips were both shut.

quiz.p: How does the sound of a struck steel plate reach a skin 10 cm away?
opts: Air particles pass the pushes along
quiz.why: The plate pushes the air next to it. Each air particle pushes the next, until the pushes reach the skin. In the Thali and the Skin, nothing but air was in between.

quiz.p: A test changes the kind of string and counts seconds of ringing. Which is the dependent variable?
quiz.why: The dependent variable is what you measure. The kind of string is the independent variable, changed on purpose. The spoon and the length are control variables.

quiz.p: A plucked string slowly goes quiet. Where has the energy of the pluck gone?
opts: Into the air as sound, and into warmth
quiz.why: Each vibration passes a little energy to the air as sound. A little more warms the string and what it touches. Energy is never destroyed.

quiz.p: Why is a veena string much louder on the veena than stretched between two hands?
opts: The wide wooden body pushes more air
The wood makes the string tighter
The wood vibrates faster than the string

applications: Makers of veenas, violins and guitars choose the wood, the thickness and the shape of the body with care. A good body vibrates well and pushes the air strongly.
A loudspeaker is a skin, called a cone, pushed back and forth by a magnet. A microphone is a skin that sound pushes, joined to something that turns the movement into an electric signal.
A quartz watch keeps time by counting the vibrations of a tiny crystal, 32,768 each second.
Engineers put rubber pads under engines, washing machines and mixer-grinders. Then less vibration passes into the floor and the walls.
Factory engineers listen to machines with vibration meters. A worn bearing changes the vibration long before the machine breaks.
A doctor's ultrasound scanner sends vibrations too fast to hear into the body, and builds a picture from the echoes.
A phone buzzes because a tiny motor spins a weight that is off its centre. Each turn gives the phone one push.

open_questions.q: How does the brain turn a row of pushes into the feeling of one note?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know which parts of the inner ear and the brain respond to each frequency. They still argue about how timing and place are combined into the note we hear.

open_questions.q: Why do cats purr, and how do they keep the purr so low?
open_questions.why_open: A 2023 study found pads inside cats' vocal folds that may slow the vibration. How a living cat controls the purr, and all that a purr is for, are still not settled.

open_questions.q: Do plants make sounds for anyone to hear?
open_questions.why_open: In 2023 a team recorded dry and cut plants giving off clicks too high for humans to hear. Nobody knows yet whether insects, other animals or other plants listen to them.

open_questions.q: Is everything, at the smallest scale, a vibration?
open_questions.why_open: String theory says so, but no experiment has been able to test it. It may stay untested for a long time.

open_questions.q: What is it like to hear a sound too low or too high for humans?
open_questions.why_open: We can measure what an elephant's or a bat's ears respond to. We have no way yet to know what the hearing is like for them.

maths.problem: In the Comb Test, a card crosses 40 teeth in 2 seconds, and then in half a second. How many ticks each second is each stroke?
maths.answer: 20 ticks each second, and then 80 ticks each second.
maths.explain: 40 ticks shared over 2 seconds is 40 ÷ 2 = 20 each second. In half a second there are 40 ticks, so a whole second would have twice as many: 40 × 2 = 80.
maths.context: In the Comb Test you draw a card along 40 teeth of a comb. A slow stroke gives separate ticks, and a quick stroke gives a note.
maths.why_maths: The number of ticks each second is something you can compare from one stroke to the next. The words 'fast' and 'slow' cannot be compared in that way.

maths.problem: In the Comb Test, the strokes gave 5, 10, 20, 40 and 80 ticks each second. What is the pattern? What stroke time would give the next number?
maths.answer: Each number is double the one before. The next is 160 ticks each second, from a stroke of a quarter of a second.
maths.explain: 5 × 2 = 10, 10 × 2 = 20, and so on, so the next is 80 × 2 = 160. The stroke times halve each time: 8, 4, 2, 1, a half, and then a quarter of a second.
maths.context: In the Comb Test you draw a card along 40 teeth of a comb. The strokes take 8, 4, 2, 1 and half a second. You listen for the ticks to turn into a note.
maths.why_maths: Seeing the doubling pattern lets you predict a stroke you have not made, and then test the prediction.

maths.problem: A mosquito's wings beat about 500 times each second. A honeybee's beat about 230 times. Whose hum is higher? How many times do the mosquito's wings beat in one minute?
maths.answer: The mosquito's hum is higher. Her wings beat about 30,000 times in one minute.
maths.explain: More pushes each second give a higher note, and 500 is more than 230. One minute is 60 seconds, and 500 × 60 = 30,000.
maths.context: The Comb Test showed that more ticks each second give a higher note. An insect's hum is made by the beats of the wings.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying shows how many separate pushes are hidden inside a hum that sounds like one steady thing.

maths.problem: In the Spoon on a String, the ring lasted 7, 8 and 9 seconds through the string. Through the air it lasted 1, 2 and 1 seconds. About how many times as long did it last through the string?
maths.explain: The string total is 7 + 8 + 9 = 24 seconds. The air total is 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 seconds. 24 ÷ 4 = 6. Both totals are for three taps, so they can be compared directly.
maths.context: In the Spoon on a String you tap a hanging spoon and count the seconds you hear the ring. You listen through the air and then through the string. These counts are made up.
maths.why_maths: Saying that the ring lasted six times as long tells you how big the difference is. Saying only that it lasted longer does not.

maths.problem: In the Thali and the Skin, the total scores were 6 at 10 cm and 5 at 20 cm. They were 2 at 40 cm and 0 at 80 cm. A friend then gets 4 at 80 cm. Is that likely to be right? Explain.
maths.answer: It is not likely. It breaks the pattern, so it should be tested again.
maths.explain: The scores fall as the distance grows: 6, 5, 2, 0. A score of 4 at 80 cm is higher than the score at 40 cm, which does not fit. A bumped table or a much harder strike could explain it. Repeating the strikes at 80 cm will show.
maths.context: In the Thali and the Skin you strike a steel plate at four distances from a skin of cling film. You score how much the grains on the skin move. These scores are made up.
maths.why_maths: A pattern in the numbers tells you which result to doubt and test again.

maths.problem: A young person hears from about 20 hertz up to about 20,000 hertz. How many times as high is the top of that range as the bottom?
maths.explain: 20,000 ÷ 20 = 1,000. The fastest vibration a young ear can hear is a thousand times as fast as the slowest.
maths.context: In the Comb Test, ticks turned into a note at about 20 each second. That is the bottom of the range humans can hear. The top is about 20,000 each second.
maths.why_maths: Dividing shows how wide the range of human hearing is, in one number.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out what makes the human voice? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: For a very long time, doctors thought the voice worked like a wind instrument. The Greek doctor Galen, about 1,800 years ago, compared the voice box to the mouthpiece of a blown pipe. On this idea the blown air made the note. In 1741 the French doctor Antoine Ferrein tested it. He took voice boxes from dead bodies and blew air through the windpipe. They gave a sound. When he stretched the two small bands inside the voice box tighter, the note rose. So the bands were vibrating, as the strings of a violin do, with the air acting like a bow. He named them vocal cords. Nobody had yet seen them move in a living person. In 1854 Manuel García, a Spanish singing teacher, held a small dentist's mirror at the back of his own throat. He used a second mirror to shine sunlight on it. He saw his vocal cords open and close as he sang. Today we know they are soft folds and not strings. Breath blows them apart, and they spring shut again.
how_we_found_out.who: Galen, a Greek doctor in Rome, Antoine Ferrein, a French doctor, and Manuel García, a Spanish singing teacher
how_we_found_out.when: Galen wrote about 1,800 years ago. Ferrein reported his tests in 1741. García saw his own vocal cords in 1854 and reported it in 1855.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the voice is like a flute, with only the air in the windpipe making the note. Ferrein showed that tightening the bands in the voice box raises the note, so the bands are part of the source.
how_we_found_out.art: A man in nineteenth-century clothes sitting by a sunny window, holding a small dentist's mirror in his open mouth and a hand mirror that reflects a beam of sunlight into it.

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, step by step. The experiments were reasoned through carefully, but they have not yet been tried at home. Treat the expected results as likely, and write down what really happens. The Comb Test (core) needs a comb with 40 teeth of one size, a stiff card and a stopwatch. Most people should hear separate ticks at 5 and 10 a second, and a rattle near 20. They should hear a buzz near 40 and a low note at 80. A hand cannot keep a steady speed, so each stroke is done three times. Half a second is only roughly timed. The Slow String (core) needs six rubber bands and a clothes peg. With the peg on, the chain should swing about 3 times a second. If it is too quick to follow, hold it looser or add a second peg. The Thali and the Skin (core) needs a tight, smooth film and only 20 to 30 grains of rava. The grains should jump at 10 centimetres and stay still by 80 centimetres. The distances in between will differ from home to home. The clang is loud, so the watcher covers both ears. The Spoon on a String (core) is very reliable for cotton string against air. Wool and rubber bands may give results that differ from the example table. The water step shows only that clicks cross water and the bucket wall. The Palm Pipe works best with a stiff cardboard tube. The listening part at the end is faint. The Dancing Light Spot needs a dim room and a wall 1 to 2 metres away. With a torch the spot is a fuzzy patch, and sunlight gives a sharper one. No laser pointer is used. Quiet the Buzz needs a phone that can be set to vibrate. No part needs a garden, a pet or a musical instrument. Facts checked on 17 Nov 2026 against scholarly or official sources: the papers and book citations, Hooke's toothed wheel (1681), Boyle's bell in the pumped jar, Ferrein (1741), García (1854/1855), the wingbeat, purr, voice, guitar and quartz frequencies, the Earth's 54-minute mode, the Sun's five-minute rise and fall, and the museum and website links. Softened: Galen's flute comparison (no longer says no solid part moved), Ferrein's tests (only the tightening raising the note is kept), the Boyle bell (the sound grows much fainter), Sharngadeva's chapter 1, the speed of atoms in solids, and the brass wheel.
